docs.title: dplPy
docs.text:
These docs track the development branch

This site is built from the main branch of dplPy on every push, so it may describe functions, arguments, or defaults that are not yet in the released PyPI version. The most recent release is dplPy 0.9.0 (see PyPI and the changelog). Check what you have installed with python -c "import dplpy; print(dplpy.__version__)" and upgrade with pip install --upgrade dplpy.

dplPy is the Dendrochronology Program Library for Python — an open-source toolkit for loading, standardizing, crossdating, and analyzing tree-ring width data. It is part of the OpenDendro project and is a Python companion to the R library dplR, reproducing its methods (and adding COFECHA-style crossdating) so that dendrochronologists can work in either ecosystem.

import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl")     # load ring widths
rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl)             # remove the growth trend -> indices
crn = dpl.chron(rwi)               # average into a site chronology

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Familiar to dplR users. Function names and behavior track dplR closely; see Coming from dplR for a side-by-side map.
  • Standardization with splines, negative-exponential/Hugershoff curves, regional curve standardization (rcs), signal-free (ssf), age-dependent splines (ads), and power transformation (powt).
  • Chronologies with autoregressive (chron_ars) and variance-stabilized (chron_stabilized) options.
  • Crossdating with a dplR-faithful xdate, a COFECHA emulation mode (xdate(preset="COFECHA")), a COFECHA-style batch report (xdate_report), floating-series dating (xdate_floater), and relative dating of a set of undated series against one another (xdate_undated).
  • Interchange with ITRDB Tucson .rwl/.crn files and LiPD.

docs.title: Citing dplPy
docs.text: dplPy is developed by the OpenDendro group (Andy Bunn, Kevin Anchukaitis, Tyson Swetnam, and contributors). If you use it in published work, please cite the OpenDendro project and the underlying methods referenced in each function's documentation. See the project repository for the current recommended citation.

docs.title: Crossdating: dplR vs COFECHA
docs.text: dplPy's xdate can run in two modes that emulate two different, long-established crossdating programs. They are not variations on one method — they are two distinct method families, and dplPy reproduces each within its own family. This page explains the difference and shows how closely dplPy tracks each reference.

docs.title: Two method families
docs.text:
Default (preset=None) preset="COFECHA" Emulates dplR corr.rwl.seg the COFECHA program Correlation Spearman (rank) Pearson Prewhitening Yule-Walker AR Burg (maximum-entropy) AR Master series biweight, leave-one-out arithmetic, z-scored, leave-one-out Detrending of series as supplied (dplR-style) spline variance stabilization Critical value p-value threshold (p_val) COFECHA's t-based critical-r table Segments dplR bins COFECHA segment anchoring A flag (weak correlation) yes (reproduces dplR) yes B flag (lag shift) yes (COFECHA-style) yes

The default is the right choice when you want dplR-comparable results; the COFECHA preset is for reproducing (or submitting alongside) a COFECHA run. The Crossdating & COFECHA guide shows how to call each.

docs.title: How closely does each track its reference?
docs.text:
A useful test is to run one collection through all the relevant programs. On wa082 (Hurricane Ridge, Abies amabilis, a public ITRDB collection), the series intercorrelation lands as follows:

Run Series intercorrelation dplR corr.rwl.seg 0.564 dplPy preset=None 0.571 COFECHA (1996, ITRDB-posted) 0.586 COFECHA (2026, run locally) 0.600 dplPy preset="COFECHA" 0.599

Two things stand out. First, dplPy sits inside each family: preset=None reproduces dplR (0.571 vs 0.564, the small gap a detrending detail), and preset="COFECHA" reproduces the modern COFECHA run (0.599 vs 0.600), matching per-series "correlation with master" to a mean absolute difference of about 0.004. Second — and importantly — the two authoritative COFECHA runs themselves disagree (0.586 vs 0.600), because they interpret one series' data marker differently. dplPy lands as close to each reference as the references land to one another.

docs.title: "Problem segments" is a screen, not a fixed count
docs.text: The number of flagged "problem segments" is a threshold-dependent quality screen, not a fixed property of a collection. Across the five wa082 runs above it ranges from 0 to 11, driven by the significance threshold, the segment anchoring, and the flag rules — and the two COFECHA runs alone span 8 to 11. Read the flag count as "where should I look?", not as a score. The A flag marks segments whose correlation with the master is weak; the B flag marks segments that correlate better at a shifted position (a possible dating error). Both point you at segments to inspect by eye.

docs.title: Why not bit-identical?
docs.text: The residual differences from a given COFECHA binary come down to (a) how a particular program version reads non-standard data markers, and (b) small numerical choices in the AR and spline steps — not the crossdating mathematics, which reproduces per series to within a few thousandths of a correlation unit. See Fidelity & departures for the project's general stance on reproduction versus bit-identity, and References for the sources behind each method.

docs.title: Fidelity & departures
docs.text: dplPy is a port. Its goal is to reproduce the methods of the established dendrochronology tools — primarily dplR, and, where relevant, COFECHA, ARSTAN, and CRUST — so that results are comparable across ecosystems. This page explains what "reproduce" means here, how it is checked, and the places where dplPy deliberately departs from its references.

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
Two commitments guide the port:

  1. Where dplPy claims to reproduce a reference method, that claim is checked against the reference implementation — not from memory or documentation, but against the actual source.
  2. Every deliberate departure is documented at the point it occurs (in the relevant function's docstring) and summarized here.

In 2026 the crossdating and standardization stack was put through a systematic fidelity audit: every behavioral constant and every "matches dplR / COFECHA / ARSTAN" claim in the source was verified against the authoritative references — the dplR 1.8.0 R sources, the CRUST Fortran (Melvin & Briffa), and the COFECHA Fortran. Unsourced constants were removed or documented, and overstated claims were corrected.

docs.title: A note on precision
docs.text: Reproducing a method is not the same as being bit-identical to a compiled Fortran program. For pure-Python ports of dplR routines, dplPy follows dplR's algorithm step for step. For the COFECHA and ARSTAN emulations, dplPy reproduces the headline numbers closely (see Crossdating: dplR vs COFECHA) but will not match the original binaries to the last digit — the reference programs themselves differ from run to run and version to version. dplPy's documentation avoids claiming a numerical precision it cannot demonstrate.

docs.title: Documented departures
docs.text:
These are the places where dplPy intentionally differs from dplR (or from the tool it is emulating). None is accidental; each is chosen and documented.

Area Departure Why Crossdating B flag xdate flags a segment "B" when its correlation is higher at a non-dated lag. dplR 1.8.0's corr.rwl.seg runs the same lag search (lag.max, best.lag/best.rho) and plot.crs tints lag segments, but keeps its returned flags significance-only; dplPy promotes that lag result to an explicit B flag, active in both the default and the COFECHA preset. COFECHA's lag-shift information is useful; it is provided in both modes by design. Floating-series match xdate_floater selects the best placement by the highest t statistic; dplR's xdate.floater uses the highest correlation r. dplPy also omits dplR's future-year trim. t accounts for the degrees of freedom at each overlap (e.g. Wilson 2026). RCS / SSF preset="crust" A minimum curve-value floor of 0.02 is applied. This comes from CRUST (Melvin & Briffa 2014), not from dplR's rcs/ssf. It reproduces the CRUST behavior the preset is meant to emulate. chron_ars ARSTAN chronology The ars column defaults to ars_method="arstan": the residual chronology is re-reddened with the pooled AR coefficients (ARSTAN's albino1 then commie1, and the development version of dplR since October 2026), whereas released dplR up to 1.8.0 re-reddens each series and then averages. ars_method="dplr" restores that order. Re-reddening initials follow ARSTAN's bckcst, not dplR's postAR. chron_ars emulates ARSTAN, so its ARSTAN chronology follows Ed Cook's Fortran. The two constructions diverge under changing sample depth (ca533: max difference about 0.25). stabilize_chron / stabilize= rescaling The stabilized chronology is restandardized to the input's full-period mean and SD, not to a user-chosen reference period as in ARSTAN's stabbm. Keeps the stabilized chronology on the same overall scale as the input without requiring a reference-period choice, while the time-varying variance is still removed. powt power vs ARSTAN The adaptive power is fit by regressing log(spread) on log(level) across adjacent rings. dplPy (following dplR) uses the pair mean (x[t]+x[t-1])/2 as the level and applies p = |1-b| unclamped; ARSTAN's option 4 uses the trailing ring x[t] as the level and clamps p to [0, 1]. dplPy reproduces dplR's powt exactly (its primary reference); a series' power can therefore differ slightly from ARSTAN's. AR order selection autoreg, ar_func and every prewhiten=True path fit Yule-Walker AR models (as R's ar() does) but choose the order at the first local AIC minimum with a cap of ar_max=10 (first_aic_min=True), the ARSTAN/COFECHA rule. R's ar() and dplR take the global AIC minimum up to 10·log10(n). One package-wide prewhitening default, matching the Fortran programs dplPy emulates. first_aic_min=False (and ar_max=None where offered) reproduce R's choice. detrend negative spline period A negative spline_period is read as a percent spline (|spline_period|/100 × n). The ARSTAN convention. dplR simply rejects non-positive stiffness. writers Interior gaps indicated by a negative default value of -99 on write, a dplPy convention but similar to other applications), and the default precision is 0.001 (dplR defaults to 0.01). This convention is explicit, human-readable, and reversible. readers Anomalous negative values (but not the -9999 stop marker) are set to NaN with a warning rather than silently altered; *-noaa.rwl template files are rejected with an informative error. Ring widths cannot be negative and negative values (except the stop value) are meant to indicate gaps in the data.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text: Each function's docstring states its reference and any departure; the API Reference surfaces those docstrings directly. The crossdating method families — the largest and most consequential area of emulation — have their own page: Crossdating: dplR vs COFECHA. The works behind these methods are collected in References.

docs.title: Reconstruction validation
docs.text: A climate reconstruction is a model — tree-ring predictors mapped onto a climate target over a period where both are known, then extrapolated to centuries where only the tree rings exist. The question that matters is not whether the model fits the years it was built on, but whether it has genuine skill on years it has never seen. This page explains how pcreg answers that question, what each statistic means, and where dplPy follows or departs from the method in Ed Cook's OSR program (Cook, Briffa & Jones 1994).

docs.title: A note on the word
docs.text: dplPy says validation, not "verification". The distinction follows Oreskes, Shrader-Frechette & Belitz (1994): to verify (Latin verus, true) is to establish truth, which is possible only in a closed system. A reconstruction is a model of an open natural system, so its truth can never be established — only its legitimacy. "Validation" denotes exactly that, and it is the honest word for what these statistics do. dplPy's API reflects this: the withheld window is the validation= argument, and the result carries .validation. (Cook's Fortran subroutine is named verify; references to that routine keep its original name.)

docs.title: Split-sample validation
docs.text:
The design is simple and strict. The overlap between the predictors and the climate target is divided into a calibration period, where the model is built (screen → PCA → regression → back-transform), and a validation period of withheld years the model never saw during fitting. Skill is judged only on the withheld years.

In dplPy the two windows are stated explicitly:

import dplpy as dpl
res = dpl.pcreg(predictors, target,
                calibration=(1965, 1989),
                validation=(1959, 1964))

Cook's Fortran derives the validation period automatically as every overlap year outside the calibration window (a block before and a block after). dplPy deliberately requires the analyst to state it instead. The reason is data quality: an instrumental target may be unreliable in part of its record — a gridded PDSI that relaxes toward climatology before the dense-station era, say — and blindly validating against those years would inflate or wreck the skill for reasons that have nothing to do with the reconstruction. An explicit window lets a knowledgeable analyst fence off bad data; it is a control worth keeping.

docs.title: Calibration-period skill is not validation
docs.text: The calibration R² (result.cal_r2) — the fraction of target variance the model explains in sample — is reported, but it is a floor, not a verdict. A model with many predictors screened over few years can fit the calibration period well and still have no out-of-sample skill. The validation statistics exist precisely because calibration fit can mislead.

docs.title: The validation statistics
docs.text:
All of the following are computed on the withheld years, in result.stats, for both the raw series and (see below) its first differences.

Reduction of Error (RE) is the central statistic. It compares the reconstruction's error against the error of simply guessing the calibration mean every year:

RE = 1 − Σ(observed − reconstructed)² / Σ(observed − calibration_mean)²

RE runs from −∞ to 1. Anything above 0 means the reconstruction beats climatology on the withheld years. It is a sensitive test — a low bar, and the usual minimum threshold for claiming any skill.

Coefficient of Efficiency (CE) is the same ratio with a stricter baseline: the validation-period mean rather than the calibration mean.

CE = 1 − Σ(observed − reconstructed)² / Σ(observed − validation_mean)²

Because the validation-period mean is the best constant predictor for those years, CE is harder to pass, and \(\mathrm{CE} \le \mathrm{RE}\) in general. The gap between them reflects how much the calibration and validation means differ; a positive CE is the stronger claim of skill.

Correlations. Pearson r measures linear agreement; Spearman and Kendall are rank-based and insensitive to a few outliers; the robust correlation is the biweight midcorrelation, which down-weights outliers directly. Each is reported with a one-sided significance (_p) — a valid reconstruction is expected to correlate positively, so the test is one-tailed.

Sign test counts how many withheld years place the actual and the reconstruction on the same side of the mean, against a 50/50 coin — pure directional agreement. The product-means test (Fritts) is a weighted version, asking whether the same-sign agreements dominate. The equality-of-means test is a Welch t-test that the reconstruction is not biased — that its mean over the withheld years matches the actual mean.

docs.title: High-frequency skill: the first-difference pass
docs.text: Every statistic is computed a second time on the year-to-year differences of both series (the _diff keys in result.stats). This is the stricter view. A reconstruction can look excellent on levels purely by sharing a low-frequency trend with the target, while having no real interannual skill. Differencing removes the trend and asks whether the reconstruction tracks the wiggles. Strong level agreement with weak differenced agreement is a warning that the skill is all in the trend.

docs.title: Cross-validation
docs.text: Split-sample validation uses one withheld window. Cross-validation (cv=) instead rotates the held-out years through the calibration period: with cv=1 it leaves out one year at a time (leave-one-out), with cv=k it leaves out contiguous k-year blocks, and — crucially — it refits the entire pipeline (screening, PCA, regression) on the remaining years each time before predicting the held-out ones. The pooled held-out predictions give cv_r, cv_RE and cv_CE. Because nothing from a held-out year informs its own prediction, cross-validation exposes overfitting that the in-sample R² hides: a model that screens hundreds of predictors over a few decades can show a high calibration R² and a negative cv_RE.

docs.title: What dplPy implements, and where it departs from Cook's OSR
docs.text:
dplPy reproduces Cook's validation design — split-sample, the full statistical panel, RE against the calibration mean and CE against the validation mean, and the first-difference pass — and it was checked number-for-number against the compiled OSR Fortran on a single-target fixture. It then makes a few deliberate, documented departures, all in the direction of correctness over exact reproduction (see Fidelity & departures for the package-wide principle):

Area dplPy Cook's OSR Why Significance SciPy's exact distributions Wilson-Hilferty / normal approximations The approximations are era-driven and visibly off at low degrees of freedom; a close-call predictor can land the other side of a screening threshold, but exact reproduction of a 1990s approximation is not the goal. Robust correlation Biweight midcorrelation (Wilcox; = astropy's) Ed's sum/difference biweight construction The biweight midcorrelation is the documented, standard robust correlation. Validation window Explicit validation= Auto-derived from the calibration/data overlap Analyst control over data quality (above). Cross-validation Leave-k-out refitting the whole pipeline A 301-sample bootstrap of the final pairs A refit CV is the rigorous out-of-sample test; the bootstrap resamples the fitted pairs only. Precision float64 throughout real*4 dplPy never down-casts to reproduce single-precision rounding.

Two features of the Fortran are intentionally not ported: the automatic two-block (pre- and post-calibration) validation split — a single explicit window plus cross-validation covers the practical need — and canonical regression, which is deferred.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text: The pcreg API reference documents every statistic in result.stats. The method and the works behind these statistics are collected in References.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The methods dplPy implements come from the published dendrochronology literature and from four established software tools. The works below are those cited across the dplPy source; each function's docstring names the specific reference(s) behind it, and the API Reference surfaces those docstrings directly.

docs.title: Fundamentals
docs.text:
Two foundational texts underpin the field and the methods dplPy implements:

  • Fritts, H.C. (1976). Tree Rings and Climate. Academic Press, New York.
  • Cook, E.R., Kairiukstis, L.A. (eds.) (1990). Methods of Dendrochronology: Applications in the Environmental Sciences. Springer, Dordrecht, Netherlands.

docs.title: Citing dplPy
docs.text:
dplPy is developed by the OpenDendro group. If you use it in published work, please cite the software using its archived Zenodo record, and also cite the specific method reference(s) named in the docstrings of the functions you relied on (e.g. Osborn et al. 1997 and Frank et al. 2006 for variance stabilization, Cook 1985 / ARSTAN for chron_ars).

The software has a concept DOI that always resolves to the latest release:

10.5281/zenodo.22695105

Each release also has its own version DOI on Zenodo, so you can cite the exact version you used. A suggested citation (adjust the version and year to the release you used):

Anchukaitis, K. J., Ale, I., Bunn, A. G., Swetnam, T. L., & Cook, E. R. (2026). dplPy: Dendrochronology Program Library for Python (version 0.7.0) [Computer software]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695105

In BibTeX:

@software{dplpy,
  author  = {Anchukaitis, Kevin J. and Ale, Ifeoluwa and Bunn, Andrew G. and
             Swetnam, Tyson Lee and Cook, Edward R.},
  title   = {dplPy: Dendrochronology Program Library for Python},
  year    = {2026},
  version = {0.7.0},
  doi     = {10.5281/zenodo.22695105},
  url     = {https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy}
}

The repository ships a CITATION.cff, so GitHub's "Cite this repository" button gives the current APA and BibTeX entries automatically, and always reflects the latest authors, version, and DOI.

docs.title: Crossdating tree-ring data with dplPy¶
docs.text:
Crossdating is the step that makes a tree-ring collection usable: it confirms that every ring is assigned to the exact calendar year in which it grew. A single missing or false ring throws off the dating of every older ring by a year, so before any climate or ecological analysis the collection has to be checked ring by ring.

Behind every tool here is one idea, the leave-one-out master. To test one series, dplPy averages all the other series into a master chronology and correlates the series against it. A correctly dated series tracks the master closely. A misdated segment drifts out of step, and the pattern of that drift shows where and how the dating went wrong.

This notebook walks through the full set of crossdating tools in dplPy:

  • reading and detrending a collection
  • the mean interseries correlation
  • testing each series with xdate
  • the overview plot
  • locating a simulated dating error
  • dating a floating (undated) series and rejoining it
  • emulating the classic COFECHA program
  • batch QA reports
  • and dpl.check, which screens a collection for data problems that are not dating errors

dplR users will recognize this workflow from corr.rwl.seg, corr.series.seg, and ccf.series.rwl. Every example uses the sample files in ../tests/data/rwl/, so the notebook runs as-is from the notebooks/ folder of the repository.

docs.title: 1. Reading and detrending a collection¶
docs.text:
Crossdating compares the shared year-to-year signal between trees, so the first step is to remove each series' own biological growth trend. A young tree grows wide rings that narrow with age, and that slow trend is unique to each tree. Left in, it would swamp the common climate signal that crossdating relies on.

Detrending divides each measured series by a smooth curve fitted to it, leaving a dimensionless ring-width index (RWI) that hovers around 1.0 and carries the high-frequency signal. This is the same detrending used for standardization (see the detrending guide); here we use a spline, in the spirit of COFECHA's 32-year default.

We start with ca533, a bristlecone pine collection from Campito Mountain that ships with both dplR and dplPy.

docs.title: 2. Mean interseries correlation¶
docs.text:
The single most useful number for a collection is its mean interseries correlation: the average, across all series, of how well each one correlates with the master built from the others. COFECHA prints this as the overall interseries correlation, and a value around 0.5 or higher is typical of a well-dated, climate-sensitive site.

interseries_corr takes the raw ring widths, not the detrended indices. It prewhitens and normalizes internally, the way COFECHA does.

docs.title: 3. Testing each series with xdate¶
docs.text:
xdate is the workhorse. It slides a window along each series, correlates each window against the leave-one-out master, and flags the windows that look wrong:

  • flag A means the window does not correlate significantly with the master, so it is weak or possibly misdated.
  • flag B means the window correlates better at a non-zero lag than at lag 0, the classic signature of a dating shift.

The flag report prints as it runs. The full results come back in a dictionary, including a per-series correlation table and a count of possible problems.

docs.title: 4. The crossdating overview plot¶
docs.text:
xdate_plot draws the whole collection at a glance. Each series is a horizontal bar across its calendar extent:

  • green is the series' full span.
  • blue is a segment that dates well.
  • red is a flagged segment to inspect.

A healthy collection is almost all blue. The red segments are where to look next.

docs.title: 5. Locating a dating error¶
docs.text:
The most common real error is a missing ring. In a dry year a tree may grow a ring so thin it was never measured. Every ring older than the gap then gets labeled one year too young, and the series slips out of step with the master over its older half.

Following Andy Bunn's dplR crossdating workshop, we simulate exactly that on the co021 collection. We deliberately corrupt series 644222: remove its ring for the year 1600, as if it had been missed while measuring, and prepend an NaN so the series keeps its length while every ring older than 1600 shifts a year too young.

docs.title: 6. Drilling into the flagged series¶
docs.text:
series_corr zooms in on one series. The lag panel is the key part: for each window it shows the lag at which the window best matches the master.

For a missing ring, every window older than the gap correlates best at lag +1, while younger windows sit at lag 0. The year where the lag jumps from 0 to +1 is the year the ring was missed. The error is located, not just detected.

docs.title: 7. Dating a floating series¶
docs.text:
Sometimes a series carries no calendar dates at all, such as a beam from an old building or a subfossil log. Given a dated reference collection, xdate_floater finds where the floating series belongs in time.

Here we take one series from ca533, throw away its dates, and recover them.

docs.title: Rejoining the placed series¶
docs.text:
With return_rwl=True, xdate_floater hands back the floater already dated at its best-fit years as fl["placed"]. We pass that straight to combine_rwl, which merges it into the reference collection on the union of their years, exactly as dplR's combine.rwl does. Because the placement is correct, the recovered CAM021 lands back on its original years and the rejoined collection matches the one we started with.

(xdate_floater also returns fl["combined"], the same rejoin done for you, when you do not need the two pieces separately.)

docs.title: 8. Emulating COFECHA¶
docs.text:
COFECHA (Holmes, 1983) is the Fortran program that has been the standard crossdating check for decades. preset="COFECHA" reproduces its exact recipe: a 32-year spline detrend, autoregressive prewhitening using the Burg method, an arithmetic z-scored master, Pearson instead of Spearman correlation, and COFECHA's segment anchoring and critical value.

Unlike the default path, the preset expects to take the raw ring widths and detrends them itself, just as the COFECHA Fortran program did, so there is no need to call detrend first.

docs.title: 9. Batch QA reports¶
docs.text:
xdate_report runs the whole crossdating check on a file and produces a COFECHA-style text report, built for screening many files at once. It accepts a file path or a collection already read into memory.

output= controls where the report goes: "screen" prints it, "file" writes a .txt, and "both" (the default) does both. We use "screen" here so the notebook does not leave files behind.

docs.title: 10. Integrity checks with dpl.check¶
docs.text:
Crossdating asks whether every ring is on its correct year. dpl.check asks a different question: does the data make sense at all? It screens a collection for problems that are not dating errors and returns them as a table of findings, one row per problem.

Each finding carries:

  • series -- the series it concerns, blank for a whole-collection or file-level finding. In crossdating you think series-first: which cores are fine and which need a look.
  • check -- a stable id for the kind of problem, matching dplR's rwl.check ids, such as RWL_INTERNAL_NA or RWL_SERIES_OUTLIER.
  • severity -- error, warning, or note, so you can triage at a glance.
  • group -- the family the check belongs to: structure, series, values, zeros, crossdating, file, or provenance.
  • year_from, year_to, n -- where the problem sits in the series and how many rings it spans.
  • value -- a number attached to the finding, such as a correlation or a lag.
  • message -- a plain-English description.

The checks cover missing values inside a series, duplicated cores, a constant value used as a not-measured placeholder (a real ITRDB hazard, like someone entering 1 for a ring that was never measured), implausible means or units, locally absent rings, file-format defects, and the crossdating screen itself.

check and the dating tools complement each other. Where xdate and series_corr locate a dating error, check flags the same series from a different angle. Run it on the collection with the simulated missing ring, and the corrupted series turns up as a poor-fit crossdating outlier.

docs.title: Where to go next¶
docs.text:
That is the full crossdating toolkit: a collection-wide number (interseries_corr), a per-series test (xdate), a visual overview (xdate_plot), a per-series drill-down (series_corr), floating-series placement and rejoining (xdate_floater, combine_rwl), COFECHA emulation (preset="COFECHA"), batch reports (xdate_report), and a data-integrity screen (dpl.check).

  • For the detrending step behind the indices, see the detrending and standardization guide.
  • For how dplPy's crossdating compares with COFECHA and dplR, see the crossdating background note.
  • For building chronologies from a crossdated, detrended collection, see the chronologies guide.

The four chronologies agree on the high-frequency, year-to-year signal and diverge mostly (although still minimally) in the low-frequency trend — which is exactly where the method choice matters. Signal-free standardization and multiple curves each adjust the long-term shape, and the differences you see are the sample-bias corrections those methods are designed to make.

docs.title: Regional Curve Standardization with dplPy¶
docs.text:
Most detrending fits a separate growth curve to each series and divides it out. That works for closed-canopy, uniform-age stands, but it has a cost: a curve fit to one series cannot tell a slow climate trend from the tree's own growth trend, so it removes both. Any climate signal longer than the individual segments is lost. This is the segment-length curse.

Regional Curve Standardization (RCS) breaks the curse. Instead of one curve per series, it aligns every series by cambial age (rings counted from the pith), averages them into a single regional curve that describes the average biological growth trend for the site, and divides each series by the slice of that one curve matching its own ages. Because the regional curve is common to all trees, climate trends longer than any single series survive. RCS is the method of choice for long, composite, and subfossil collections, where recovering multi-centennial climate is the whole point.

dplPy offers four members of the RCS family:

  • rcs — the classic single regional curve.
  • sfrcs — signal-free RCS, which removes the common climate signal's imprint on the regional curve before standardizing.
  • mrcs — multiple-curve RCS, one regional curve per growth-rate class.
  • sfmrcs — signal-free multiple-curve RCS, the two ideas combined.

This notebook works through all four on a real subfossil collection: the Taimyr (TAI) Siberian larch set from Büntgen et al. (2021), read straight from the ITRDB. It is 356 series spanning 207 BC to AD 2011 — exactly the kind of long, composite material RCS is built for. Along the way we poke the functions a little, since they are new.

docs.title: 1. Read the collection from the ITRDB¶
docs.text: readers takes a URL, so we pull the Taimyr file directly from the NOAA archive. Swap the site code in the URL for another Büntgen 2021 site (for example NYA_all.rwl, the largest) to run the same notebook on different data.

docs.title: 2. Check for oddities¶
docs.text: Before standardizing anything, screen the collection with dpl.check. For a subfossil larch set we expect a lot of zero rings (locally absent rings, a real and common feature of these trees), so those show up as notes, not errors.

docs.title: 3. Verify the collection crossdates¶
docs.text: These are published, already-crossdated data, so this is a sanity check rather than a re-dating. The mean interseries correlation is the single number that summarizes how strongly the series share a common signal; a healthy site sits around 0.5 or higher.

docs.title: 4. A note on pith offsets¶
docs.text:
RCS aligns series by cambial age, so in principle it needs each series' pith offset — how many rings are missing between the innermost measured ring and the true pith. This file ships no offset table, so we use dplPy's default: every series is treated as pith-present (po=0), aligning by the first measured ring. That is the standard fallback when offsets are not archived, and it is what most published RCS chronologies without pith estimates assume.

If you do have offsets, pass them as po= (a {series: offset} map or a two-column table). dplPy's pith_offset is a true offset: 0 means the pith is present. (dplR's po is the cambial age of the first ring, where 1 means pith present, so subtract 1 from a dplR table.)

docs.title: 5. rcs: the single regional curve¶
docs.text: rcs fits one regional curve to the age-aligned collection and divides each series by it. The defaults are dplPy's modern choices: an age-dependent spline for the curve (fit="AgeDepSpline"), the ratio method (method="ratio"), and a non-increasing old-age end (pos_slope=False, faithful to ARSTAN and CRUST). plot=True draws dplPy's RCS figure: the regional curve and the resulting chronology.

docs.title: Poking rcs: ratio vs difference, and the old-age slope¶
docs.text: Two switches are worth seeing. method="difference" subtracts the curve instead of dividing by it (the variance-stabilized choice); pos_slope=True lets the regional curve rise again at great age instead of being held non-increasing. We compare the regional curves under the default and pos_slope=True.

docs.title: 6. sfrcs: signal-free RCS¶
docs.text:
There is a subtlety in RCS. The regional curve is an average over all series, so a strong common climate signal leaves its fingerprint in the curve itself, which then gets divided back out of the indices — biasing the result, especially the low-frequency trend and the recent end where sample depth changes. Signal-free standardization (Melvin & Briffa) breaks the circularity: it estimates the curve, removes the common signal, re-estimates the curve from the signal-free series, and iterates until the curve stops changing.

sfrcs runs that iteration around the RCS curve.

docs.title: The signal-free curve, side by side¶
docs.text: Plotting the two regional curves together shows what the signal-free pass changed. On TAI the curves are close, so the common signal left only a modest imprint, but they separate at the young, fast-growth end, where the signal-free estimate sits a little higher. That difference is small in millimetres yet it is exactly the kind of low-frequency adjustment that carries through into the chronology.

docs.title: 7. mrcs: multiple regional curves¶
docs.text:
A single regional curve assumes every tree follows the same average growth trend. But fast- and slow-growing trees have differently shaped curves, and if the mix of fast- and slow-growers changes over time — as it does when a subfossil collection shifts from one period to another — a single average curve injects a spurious trend. This is modern (or differing-contemporaneous) sample bias.

mrcs (the CRUST approach of Melvin & Briffa) sorts the trees by growth rate, splits them into n_curves equal classes, and builds one regional curve per class. Each tree is standardized by the curve for its own class.

docs.title: 8. sfmrcs: signal-free multiple-curve RCS¶
docs.text: The two refinements are independent, so they combine: sfmrcs runs the signal-free iteration around the multiple-curve allocation. It is the most elaborate member of the family.

docs.title: 9. The family nests¶
docs.text: mrcs and sfmrcs are strict generalizations: with a single class they must reduce exactly to rcs and sfrcs. This is both a design property worth knowing and a correctness check worth running.

docs.title: 10. Comparing the four chronologies¶
docs.text: The real test is what the chronologies look like. We build a standard chronology from each set of indices with chron, then overlay them. To see the low-frequency behaviour — the part RCS exists to preserve — we smooth each with a 20-year running mean and show the well-replicated portion (sample depth at least five series).

docs.title: Choosing among them¶
docs.text:
• rcs — the baseline. One regional curve, the method's original form.
  • sfrcs — when you want to remove the common signal's bias from the curve, especially for the low-frequency trend and the recent end.
  • mrcs — when the growth-rate mix of the sample changes through time, which risks a spurious trend from a single blended curve.
  • sfmrcs — both corrections at once.

All four share the same fit, method, period, and pos_slope vocabulary as detrend and rcs, so anything you learned tuning one carries over. Pith offsets, when you have them, go in po= and matter most for the shape of the young end of every curve.

See the detrending and standardization guide for the curve-fitting options, and the fidelity notes for how dplPy's RCS follows ARSTAN and CRUST.

Two series carry a run of the same value, 0.01 mm, for several years in a row. A larch ring of 0.01 mm is not a real measurement. It is the smallest nonzero value the file can hold, and here it stands in for something else. Across the whole file the value 0.01 turns up 217 times in 24 series, so this is a convention, not a typo.

What does it mean? There are two likely readings, and the file does not say which:

  • a not-measured value, a gap in the record, or
  • a locally absent ring written as a tiny number because some detrending programs historically refused a literal 0.

Let us look at one of the flagged series.

Real ring widths sit on both sides of this run of inplausible measurements. That is the case fill_internal is built for. First we mark every 0.01 placeholder as not-measured (NaN), which turns each run into an interior gap. Then fill_internal estimates the gap so the series can be used by tools that reject interior gaps, such as detrend and the crossdating checks. In the code below, we use fill="ARSTAN" to call on Ed Cook's spline based infilling method, which uses information from series with non-missing measurements to help estimate the missing values. Other options (inherited from dplR) include Spline,Mean,and Linear. See here for more: https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/utilities/#fill_internal

If instead we judged these to be locally absent rings, the right action would be to set them to 0, which dplPy keeps as real data rather than a gap. The choice is the analyst's. Here we take the not-measured reading.

In [14]: Copied! 
# mark the 0.01 placeholder as not-measured, then fill the interior gaps
gaps = che.mask(che == 0.01)
filled_linear = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="Linear") # linear interpolation infilling
filled_arstan = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="ARSTAN") # use Ed Cook's spline-based ARSTAN infilling
# mark the 0.01 placeholder as not-measured, then fill the interior gaps gaps = che.mask(che == 0.01) filled_linear = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="Linear") # linear interpolation infilling filled_arstan = dpl.fill_internal(gaps, fill="ARSTAN") # use Ed Cook's spline-based ARSTAN infilling

The placeholder run is gone, replaced by a smooth estimate that follows the neighboring rings. fill also accepts "Mean", "Linear", "ARSTAN", or a fixed number if you prefer a different estimate. A plot shows the repair in context.

docs.title: Reading tree-ring data with dplPy¶
docs.text:
This notebook provides a tour through the capababilities of dplpy.readers(), which reads Tucson format .rwl files (and .csv) into a Pandas DataFrame. This dataframe has one column for each measurement series, indexed by year. The full description of readers can be found in the documentation here: https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/io/#readers and the User Guide here: https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/guide/reading-writing-data/#ring-width-files-with-readers.

This notebook uses the sample files shipped in ../tests/data/rwl/ and ../tests/data/csv/, so it runs as-is from the notebooks/ folder of the repository.

First, we'll import dplPy:

docs.title: The Basics¶
docs.text: At its most simple, you can pass a filename (and path) and get back a year-indexed DataFrame with one column per series. We'll call dpl.stats as well, to give us a quick look at the data that is now in our workspace.

docs.title: Headers are detected automatically and read attributes are recorded¶
docs.text: dplPy automatically identifies where the data rows actually start and records how many header lines it skipped onin df.attrs. The .attrs is once again a feature of Pandas (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.attrs.html) that can store attributes for the dataset, so that this information is carried along throughout your script. readers uses .attrs to store anything unusual during the import process as well as metadata:

docs.title: Metadata in the header is identified and saved¶
docs.text: The site and sample metadata is parsed as best as possible from the header by dpl.readers and is saved into df.attrs["dplpy_metadata"]. Alternatively we provide dpl.metadata() which allows you to simply extract the metadata into a Python dict structure:

docs.title: Data-quality warnings and heads-up¶
docs.text: readers reads the file but flags spots worth a human's examination. For instance, a short interior gap (a missing year inside a series not indicated by a negative number), or characters past the last data column (indicating a possibly truncated value). Once again, this information is stored in df.attrs:

docs.title: Reading directly from the ITRDB¶
docs.text: readers allows you to directly read Tucson formatted tree-ring data from a URL, including from the ITRDB. In the example below, a Pinus echinata site from Oklahoma collected by Dave Stahle is fetched from the ITRDB, and readers warns the user that there is a likely formatting error that should be examined:

docs.title: A detective story: catching and repairing an oddity¶
docs.text:
Reading from the ITRDB is also where surprises turn up. Here is a real one. This European larch site from Mattertal, Switzerland (Hartl and colleagues, ITRDB che413) reads cleanly, but it carries a quirk that dpl.check is built to catch. It is important to practice safe ITRDBing!

dpl.check is the data-quality companion to readers: it screens a collection and returns problems as a table, one row per finding, each with a severity.

docs.title: Duplicate IDs merged from separate segments¶
docs.text: When a series ID appears more than once but do not have overlapping years of data, readers mimics dplR and joins them into a single series and reports the merge to the user. The idea of this default is that duplicate ID series that do not overlap in time are likely to reflect a single sample that needed to be measured in pieces (e.g due to damage, compression wood, etc.). However, if this is not the case, you can change this default behavior by setting join=False:

docs.title: Poorly formated Tucson files fail informatively (the strict=True default)¶
docs.text: Rather than take heroic measures to read an .rwl file and potentially silently corrupt the data, in default mode readers fails to read the broken file and exits with a specific and actionable message identifying the questionable series and the year. This default behavior is set by strict=True:

docs.title: Salvage mode will do everything it can to read as much of the file (strict=False)¶
docs.text: For batch processing, setting strict=False tells readers to recover whatever it reasonably can instead of failing. It may drop an unusable series and salvage the rest, it can join or rename duplicate IDs, and it records every decision and action in df.attrs["dplpy_salvage"].

docs.title: readers handles mixed measurement precision just fine¶
docs.text: A single Tucson file can have series measured at different precisions. In this example, all the TMS* cores at 0.001 mm and all the TWM* were measured at 0.01 mm many years earlier. readers automatically scales each correctly:

docs.title: Non-ASCII series IDs are handled correctly¶
docs.text: Series IDs containing non-ASCII characters are preserved as-is:

docs.title: readers also imports CSV files¶
docs.text: readers also reads year-indexed CSV ring-width files:

docs.title: Documentation¶
docs.text: The complete documentation is available in the dplPy documentation here: https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/io/#readers

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: dplPy requires Python 3.11 or newer. Its core scientific dependencies (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, matplotlib, statsmodels, csaps) are installed automatically.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
pip install dplpy

Then confirm the install:

import dplpy as dpl
print(dpl.__version__)

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
LiPD import/export is built on pylipd, which most users do not need, so it is an optional extra:

pip install "dplpy[lipd]"

docs.title: Install with conda / mamba
docs.text:
If you prefer a conda environment, create one with Python 3.11+ and install dplPy into it with pip:

conda create -n dplpy python=3.11
conda activate dplpy
pip install dplpy

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
To work from the latest main (unstable) or to contribute:

git clone https://github.com/OpenDendro/dplPy.git
cd dplPy
pip install -e .

The project develops on main, with tagged pre/releases branched from it and published to PyPI. See the repository for the current version and release notes.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Head to the Quickstart for a complete worked example, or dive into the User Guide.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This walkthrough takes a raw ring-width file all the way to a crossdated site chronology. It uses ca533.rwl (Campito Mountain bristlecone pine), one of the classic dplR/ITRDB example collections. Every code block shows real dplPy output.

docs.title: 1. Load ring widths
docs.text:
import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)

ca533.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 34 series covering the period from 626 to 1983

readers returns a pandas DataFrame indexed by year, one column per series:

rwl.shape          # (1358, 34)  -> 1358 years, 34 series

docs.title: 3. Detrend (standardize)
docs.text:
Remove each series' biological growth trend to produce ring-width index (RWI) series. The default is a smoothing spline:

rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="spline")

See Detrending & standardization for the other curves (ModNegExp, ModHugershoff, Mean, AgeDepSpline) and the rcs, ssf, ads, and powt methods.

docs.title: 4. Build a chronology
docs.text:
Average the detrended series into a site chronology. By default this is a Tukey's-biweight robust mean with a sample-depth column:

crn = dpl.chron(rwi)
crn.tail(3)

           std  samp_depth
Year
1981  1.252329          21
1982  1.362052          21
1983  1.314605          21

For AR-modelled or variance-stabilized chronologies, see Building chronologies.

docs.title: 5. Crossdate
docs.text:
xdate correlates each series, segment by segment, against a leave-one-out master to flag possible dating problems. It returns a dictionary of per-segment correlations and flags:

result = dpl.xdate(rwl)          # dplR-faithful default
result["seg_corr"]               # per-series, per-segment correlations

For a COFECHA-style run and a full formatted report, use the COFECHA preset and xdate_report:

report = dpl.xdate_report("ca533.rwl", preset="COFECHA")

The Crossdating & COFECHA guide covers flags, segment settings, the COFECHA emulation, and dating floating series with xdate_floater.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Reading & writing data
  • Coming from dplR — a function-by-function map
  • API Reference

docs.title: Building chronologies
docs.text:
A chronology averages the detrended (RWI) series into a single site record. dplPy provides two builders that sit at different points on a simplicity–fidelity spectrum:

  • chron — simple but flexible. The everyday mean-value chronology, with optional per-series prewhitening. This is the one most workflows want.
  • chron_ars — an ARSTAN emulator. Built specifically to reproduce ARSTAN's parameters and procedures: a common pooled AR order across all series, and the standard, residual, and re-reddened "ARSTAN" chronologies.

Both can also variance-stabilize their output in a single call — see Variance stabilization.

docs.title: chron: the standard chronology
docs.text:
Pass detrended series to chron:

import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)
rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="Spline")
crn = dpl.chron(rwi)
crn.tail(3)

           std  samp_depth
Year
1981  1.252329          21
1982  1.362052          21
1983  1.314605          21

The result has a std (standard chronology) column and a samp_depth (sample-depth) column, indexed by year.

  • biweight (default True) — average with Tukey's biweight robust mean rather than an arithmetic mean, reducing the influence of outlier series.
  • prewhiten (default False) — also return a residual (prewhitened) chronology in a res column. When on, the AR model is fit per series at each series' own optimal order, controlled by ar_max (default 10), aic, ar_method ("yw" Yule-Walker, the package default and R's ar() default; "burg" or "ols"), and first_aic_min (default True: the order is the first local AIC minimum, the ARSTAN/COFECHA rule; R's ar() takes the global minimum — pass first_aic_min=False to match it).
  • ci (default False) — also return bootstrap confidence limits on the mean (conf=0.95, R=100 resamples; set seed= for reproducibility).

chron is deliberately lightweight: it reproduces dplR's chron and gives you a clean standard (and optional residual) chronology without committing to ARSTAN's pooled-AR machinery. When that is all you need, it is the right tool.

docs.title: chron_ars: the ARSTAN chronology
docs.text:
chron_ars is not just a mean-value function with prewhitening bolted on — it is a mimic of Ed Cook's ARSTAN, and its parameters and procedures follow ARSTAN rather than dplR's chron where the two differ. It returns three chronologies with unified column names:

ars = dpl.chron_ars(rwi, ar_max=10, first_aic_min=True)
list(ars.columns)
# ['std', 'res', 'ars', 'samp_depth']
  • std — the standard chronology (the robust mean of the RWI series).
  • res — the residual chronology: each series is prewhitened with a common pooled AR(p) model, the prewhitened series are averaged, and that mean is prewhitened once more. (This pooled, common-order AR is the key difference from chron(prewhiten=True), which uses a per-series optimal order.)
  • ars — the ARSTAN chronology: the common red-noise persistence is reintroduced ("re-reddened") into the prewhitened signal, keeping the shared autoregressive structure while suppressing series-specific noise.

The pooled AR order is chosen from an autocovariance accumulated across all series and lags (Cook's pooled-AR approach), selected by AIC. prewhiten_method="ar.yw" uses Yule-Walker AR to match dplR.

docs.title: ars_method: how the ARSTAN chronology is built
docs.text:
There are two orders in which the re-reddening and averaging steps can be combined, and they do not commute when sample depth changes through time:

  • ars_method="arstan" (the default) — ars = postAR(res): re-redden the residual chronology itself, that is the mean of the prewhitened series after it has been prewhitened once more at the pooled order. This is exactly what Ed Cook's ARSTAN Fortran does (albino1 at the fixed pooled order, then commie1 with the pooled coefficients), and it is also what the development version of dplR's chron.ars has done since October 2026. dplPy defaults to this because chron_ars is an ARSTAN emulator.
  • ars_method="dplr" — ars = mean(postAR(prewhitened)): re-redden each prewhitened series, then average. This matches released dplR up to 1.8.0. Use it for parity with results produced by those versions.

The std and res chronologies, the pooled AR order, and the prewhitening are identical either way; only the ars column differs. On the ca533 example the two constructions correlate at 0.99 but differ by up to about 0.25 in individual years, so the choice is visible in the numbers. The re-reddening initials follow ARSTAN's bckcst (backcast from the start of each series), which differs from dplR's postAR only in the first few years of each series' contribution.

docs.title: backcast: keeping the first years
docs.text:
An AR(p) filter has no data for its p lagged terms at the start of a series, so the first p residuals would normally be undefined. ARSTAN avoids losing them by backcasting — synthesizing p pre-sample values by running the AR model in reverse (its bckcst routine) — at every prewhitening and re-reddening step. chron_ars does the same:

  • backcast=True (the default) — the residual and ARSTAN chronologies are full length, with no leading NaN. This matches ARSTAN, which backcasts both the per-series prewhitening and the re-prewhitening of the mean, so a young series' first p residuals are included in the robust mean rather than dropped.
  • backcast=False — the first p residuals are set to NaN, reproducing dplR's chron.ars.

The backcast values are model-based estimates, so treat the first p years as slightly less certain than the interior. This applies to the "ar.yw" path; the "arima.CSS-ML" path already returns full-length residuals.

docs.title: Variance-stabilizing a chronology
docs.text:
Both builders accept a stabilize= argument ("rbar", "spline", or "both") that adds a stabilized version of each chronology beside it:

crn = dpl.chron(rwi, prewhiten=True, stabilize="both")
# columns: std, std_vsc, res, res_vsc, samp_depth

ars = dpl.chron_ars(rwi, stabilize="both")
# columns: std, std_vsc, res, res_vsc, ars, ars_vsc, samp_depth

You can also stabilize a chronology you already built with stabilize_chron, or use the dplR-parity chron_stabilized. The full treatment — the method families, the running vs constant rbar, and the ARSTAN workflow — is on the Variance stabilization page.

docs.title: Which to use
docs.text: Use chron for a standard site chronology — it is the simplest path and covers most needs, with prewhiten=True when you also want a residual chronology. Reach for chron_ars when you specifically want ARSTAN's behavior: the pooled common-order AR model and the residual and re-reddened ARSTAN chronologies. Add stabilize= to either when changing sample depth would otherwise bias the chronology's variance through time, and use chron_stabilized when you need exact dplR chron.stabilized parity. See the Chronology reference for full parameter lists.

docs.title: Coming from dplR
docs.text:
dplPy is a Python companion to the R library dplR, and most workflows translate almost one-to-one. The biggest differences are ergonomic rather than conceptual:

  • Data structure. dplR uses a data.frame of class "rwl" (years as row names); dplPy uses a pandas DataFrame indexed by year. Same idea, same orientation (years down, series across).
  • Naming. R's dotted names become Python underscores (read.crn → read_crn, chron.ars → chron_ars).
  • Calling style. library(dplR); chron(rwi) becomes import dplpy as dpl; dpl.chron(rwi).
  • Return values. Some functions that print in R return a dict or DataFrame in dplPy (for example xdate returns a dict of segment correlations and flags).

docs.title: Detrending & standardization
docs.text: dplR dplPy Notes detrend, detrend.series detrend fit= selects Spline / ModNegExp / ModHugershoff / Mean / AgeDepSpline; spline_period= is dplR's nyrs; plot=False by default, like make.plot=FALSE for a data frame rcs rcs Curve via fit=, arithmetic via method=, stiffness via spline_period=; preset="crust" for the CRUST curve. Pith offset differs — see below. ssf ssf Signal-free; preset="crust" variant ads (age-dependent spline) ads Also detrend(fit="AgeDepSpline") powt powt Power transformation

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text: dplR dplPy Notes chron chron prewhiten=True adds the residual chronology chron.ci chron(ci=True) Bootstrap confidence interval on the standard chronology (adds lower_ci/upper_ci) chron.ars chron_ars ARSTAN-style chron.stabilized chron_stabilized Variance stabilization; winLength is window_length ar / AR modelling autoreg, ar_func Yule-Walker by default (method="yw"), as in R's ar(), with ar_max=10. Order selection differs: dplPy takes the first local AIC minimum (first_aic_min=True, the ARSTAN/COFECHA rule); R's ar() takes the global minimum. Pass first_aic_min=False to match R.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text: dplR dplPy Notes plot.rwl, plot.crn, spag.plot, seg.plot plot type= selects the plot style crossdating plots xdate(plot=True), xdate_plot, series_corr(plot=True)

docs.title: Beyond dplR
docs.text:
dplPy adds LiPD interchange, which dplR does not provide:

dplPy Notes to_lipd, from_lipd, lipd_metadata Requires the [lipd] extra

docs.title: Not yet ported
docs.text: dplPy targets the core standardization, chronology, and crossdating workflow. A few dplR capabilities are intentionally out of scope: superposed epoch analysis and the spectral and wavelet methods are better served by dedicated Python time-series packages such as Pyleoclim, so dplPy does not duplicate them. Skeleton-plot crossdating and interactive (point-and-click) detrending are not currently available. Of dplR's tabular I/O, read.sheet / write.sheet (tidy/long and delimited spreadsheet formats) are not yet ported. Check the API Reference for the current surface, and the project repository to request or contribute a port.

docs.title: A note on fidelity
docs.text: Where dplPy claims to reproduce a dplR (or COFECHA, or ARSTAN) method, the behavior is checked against those reference implementations, and deliberate departures are documented in the relevant function's docstring. The clearest example is crossdating: xdate's A flag reproduces dplR's corr.rwl.seg exactly. dplR 1.8.0 added a lag search of its own (corr.rwl.seg(lag.max=)) but reports it separately and still flags on significance alone; dplPy's B (lag-shift) flag folds that lag result into an explicit COFECHA-style flag.

docs.title: CooRecorder .pos files
docs.text:
CooRecorder (Cybis Elektronik & Data AB) stores a measured series as a .pos file: the x, y coordinates of each ring boundary along the measurement path. The usual way into dplPy would be to export those files to Tucson .rwl from CDendro and read the .rwl, but that export rounds the widths and drops the extra information the .pos file holds. dpl.read_pos reads the .pos file directly, at full precision, and keeps what the export throws away: earlywood and latewood widths, the pith coordinate and distance to pith, point labels and comments, and the raw coordinates for quality control.

read_pos requires CooRecorder 7.8 or later, the first version to record the pith coordinate.

docs.title: Reading one file or a whole directory
docs.text:
import dplpy as dpl

proj = dpl.read_pos("cores/AGL3_01A.pos")   # one file
proj = dpl.read_pos("cores/")               # or every .pos under a directory

read_pos returns a PosCollection. The whole-ring widths are a familiar year-by-series DataFrame, ready for the rest of dplPy:

rwl = proj.rwl()          # whole-ring widths (mm), years x series
ew  = proj.earlywood()    # earlywood widths, where seasonwood points were marked
lw  = proj.latewood()     # latewood widths

The per-series information CooRecorder recorded is in proj.attributes (one row per series: distance to pith, radius, outer and inner year, comment, CooRecorder version), the point-by-point geometry is in proj.coordinates, and any files that could not be read are listed in proj.not_read with a reason, so one bad file never aborts a directory read.

If you only want the ring widths, readers takes you straight there — a .pos file (or a directory of them) is detected automatically, and the attributes ride along on df.attrs["dplpy_pos_attributes"]:

rwl = dpl.readers("cores/")                 # whole-ring DataFrame
rwl = dpl.readers("cores/AGL3_01A.pos", format="pos")

docs.title: From CooRecorder to a pith offset
docs.text:
A .pos file often records an estimated distance to pith even when the pith ring itself was never measured. dpl.yrs_to_pith turns that distance into a pith offset — the estimated number of rings between the pith and the innermost measured ring — which rcs and po_to_wc consume directly:

proj = dpl.read_pos("cores/")
po   = dpl.yrs_to_pith(proj.rwl(), proj.attributes[["series", "distance_to_pith"]])
rwi  = dpl.rcs(proj.rwl(), po[["series", "pith_offset"]])

yrs_to_pith divides the distance to pith by a mean innermost ring width. With method="dist" (the default) it averages as many innermost rings as fit within that distance; with method="rings" it averages a fixed n_rings.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Dates. The outer date you assigned in CooRecorder is given to the outermost ring and years count inward. A file with no outer date is read with relative years, which is exactly what you want for an undated floating series headed for xdate_floater. One caveat you cannot automate away: CooRecorder sometimes stores an outer date you did not intend, and nothing in the file distinguishes that from a deliberate one — so sanity-check the assigned years, for example by plotting the series, before trusting them.
  • Cracks and gaps. dplPy measures around a crack (gap) marker rather than through it, so a crack does not count as growth. This can make a width differ slightly from CDendro's own .rwl export for a series with marked gaps.
  • Earlywood and latewood. Where you marked seasonwood boundaries, the ring is split into latewood (the outer part) and earlywood (the inner part), and earlywood + latewood equals the whole ring. In the ITRDB .rwl convention these are written as separate files with an e or l after the series number; here they are simply three frames you can use or ignore.
  • Point order. If points were saved out of order (a known CooRecorder export glitch), the widths for that series will be wrong. Reliable automatic detection is hard, so read_pos does not guess; instead it returns proj.coordinates, which you can plot to check that the points march cleanly along the core.

See the Input & output reference for the full read_pos and PosCollection signatures, and Utilities for yrs_to_pith.

docs.title: Crossdating & COFECHA
docs.text: Crossdating checks that every ring is assigned to its correct calendar year by correlating each series, segment by segment, against a master built from the other series. dplPy offers a dplR-faithful xdate, a COFECHA emulation (xdate(preset="COFECHA")), a COFECHA-style batch report, and floating-series dating.

docs.title: xdate: segment correlations and flags
docs.text:
import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)
result = dpl.xdate(rwl)
result["seg_corr"]     # per-series, per-segment correlations
result["flags"]        # A/B flags per series

xdate returns a dictionary — seg_corr (a series × segment correlation table), overall (each series' correlation with the master), flags, bins, n_problems, and a summary (see below). By default it follows dplR's corr.rwl.seg:

  • Prewhitening with a Yule-Walker AR model (prewhiten=True).
  • Spearman correlation (corr="spearman").
  • A biweight leave-one-out master — each series is compared against the mean of the others, so a misdated series cannot prop up its own correlation.
  • Overlapping segments of window_length years (default 50), stepped by half that, with bins floored to bin_floor (default 100).

docs.title: The summary header
docs.text: At the top of its output xdate prints a compact, COFECHA-style summary of the collection — number of dated series, master span, total rings, series intercorrelation, mean sensitivity, the count of possible-problem segments, and mean series length — and returns the same values in result["summary"] for programmatic use. Under preset="COFECHA" the intercorrelation and mean sensitivity are length-weighted, matching COFECHA's box.

docs.title: Reading the flags
docs.text:
The two flags are mutually exclusive, COFECHA-style:

  • B flag — the segment correlates better at a non-dated lag than where it is dated (its best lag ≠ 0), hinting at a possible dating shift. dplPy's B flag follows COFECHA (it fires whenever the best match is at a non-zero lag, with no extra margin). dplR 1.8.0's corr.rwl.seg runs the same lag search (lag.max, reporting best.lag and best.rho), but keeps its returned flags significance-only rather than raising a separate B flag; dplPy promotes that lag result to an explicit B flag, on in both the default and COFECHA modes.
  • A flag — the dated (lag-0) position is the best match, but its correlation is still not significant at p_val (default 0.05): a weak but correctly-placed segment. An A flag's best lag is therefore always 0.

dplR 1.8.0 computes a per-segment lag search (best.lag / best.rho) but still flags on significance alone; dplPy splits its flags into A (lag 0 is best) and B (a better lag exists), so a segment is never both. The per-segment lag table is printed for both flag kinds.

Set plot=True (or call xdate_plot) for a dplR-style crossdating plot, or use series_corr to drill into one series.

The plot shows significance only — read the text flags too

dplPy's crossdating plot colours a segment red purely on significance (the A screen) and does not mark B (lag) flags. A B-flagged segment that still dates significantly is drawn blue, so it can look fine on the plot even though xdate() reports it as a possible dating shift. (dplR 1.8.0's plot.crs does now tint lag segments when corr.rwl.seg is run with lag.max > 0; dplPy keeps the lag flags in the text report for now.) Always read the text flag report alongside the plot to catch B flags.

docs.title: COFECHA emulation
docs.text:
Passing preset="COFECHA" switches xdate to emulate the COFECHA program instead of dplR:

result = dpl.xdate(rwl, preset="COFECHA")

Pass the raw ring-width frame: unlike the default path (which expects detrended RWI), the COFECHA preset detrends the series itself — so do not call detrend first. The preset changes the crossdating machinery to match COFECHA:

  • a rigid cubic-spline detrend (32-yr, ratios) of the raw series,
  • spline variance stabilization of the detrended series,
  • Burg (maximum-entropy) AR prewhitening,
  • an arithmetic, z-scored leave-one-out master,
  • Pearson correlation,
  • COFECHA segment anchoring and t-based critical values, and
  • "omit absent rings" handling.

The dplR-faithful default is unchanged; the preset is an opt-in second mode.

docs.title: xdate_report: COFECHA-style batch reports
docs.text:
xdate_report runs one or more ITRDB files through crossdating and writes a formatted, COFECHA-style .txt report with per-series and per-segment correlations and a length-weighted summary:

report = dpl.xdate_report("ca533.rwl", preset="COFECHA")

It accepts a .rwl path, a list of them, or an already-loaded ring-width DataFrame (pass name= to label an in-memory frame); takes the same window_length / bin_floor / p_val settings as xdate; and offers both a dplR-faithful and a preset="COFECHA" mode. The output= argument controls where the report goes — "screen" prints it, "file" writes a <name>.txt, and "both" (the default) does both — and the report text is always returned in the result dictionary.

docs.title: Diagnostics for one series
docs.text:
series_corr reports the correlation of a single named series against the master segment by segment (useful when xdate flags a series and you want to see where), and interseries_corr returns the overall interseries correlation of the collection — the same headline number COFECHA reports — as a dict with the "mean" and the per-series "table".

dpl.series_corr(rwl, series_name="CAM011")
rbar = dpl.interseries_corr(rwl)
rbar["mean"]        # the headline mean interseries correlation
rbar["table"]       # per-series correlation with the leave-one-out master

series_corr shares xdate's vocabulary (window_length, bin_floor, p_val, lag for the cross-correlation lag search) and draws its two diagnostic panels by default. Its series_x switch (default False, dplR's stock series.x=FALSE) sets the lag convention of the dplR-style ccf panel so that a negative lag marks a missing ring in the series, consistent with the COFECHA-style lag table.

docs.title: Dating a floating series
docs.text:
xdate_floater places an undated (floating) series — a beam, a remnant log — against a dated reference collection by sliding it across every offset and scoring the fit:

placed = dpl.xdate_floater(reference_rwl, floating_series, series_name="beam1")
placed["best"]      # best-fit calendar placement and its statistics

It is based on dplR's xdate.floater and extended with the t statistic and additional crossdating statistics of Wilson (2026); the best placement is chosen by highest t (see the reference for the two documented departures from dplR).

docs.title: dplR vs COFECHA at a glance
docs.text:
Default (preset=None) preset="COFECHA" Emulates dplR corr.rwl.seg COFECHA Correlation Spearman Pearson Prewhitening Yule-Walker AR Burg (max-entropy) AR Master biweight, leave-one-out arithmetic, z-scored, leave-one-out Critical value p-value (p_val) COFECHA t-based table A flag yes (matches dplR) yes B flag (lag shift) yes (COFECHA-style) yes

See the Crossdating reference for every parameter.

docs.title: Detrending & standardization
docs.text: Standardization removes the low-frequency biological growth trend from each raw ring-width series, converting it to a dimensionless ring-width index (RWI) centered near 1.0 so series of different sizes and ages can be averaged into a chronology. dplPy offers the dplR curve-fitting methods plus regional curve, signal-free, age-dependent-spline, and power-transform approaches.

docs.title: detrend: curve fitting
docs.text:
detrend fits a growth curve to each series and divides (or subtracts) it out:

import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)
rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="Spline")

The fit argument selects the curve (dplR's names are the canonical spelling, and are case-insensitive):

fit Curve "Spline" (default) Cubic smoothing spline "AgeDepSpline" Age-dependent (increasing-stiffness) spline "ModNegExp" Negative exponential a·exp(b·t)+k, fit by nonlinear least squares (dplR), with a negexp → linear → mean fallback chain "NegExp" The same negative-exponential curve, fit by ARSTAN's deterministic method (Ed Cook's curve) "ModHugershoff" Hugershoff a·t^b·exp(c·t)+d, fit by nonlinear least squares (dplR) "Hugershoff" The Hugershoff curve, fit by ARSTAN's log-linearised closed form (Ed Cook's hughdi) "GeneralExp" General exponential a·t·exp(b·t) — Hugershoff with the power fixed at 1 (ARSTAN option 8) "LinearAny" (alias "Linear") Best-fit straight line, any slope (ARSTAN option 4) "LinearNegative" Best-fit line constrained to a non-positive slope, falling back to the mean if the slope is positive (ARSTAN option 5) "Mean" Horizontal line at the series mean

Two of these come as deterministic/nonlinear pairs — NegExp/ModNegExp and Hugershoff/ModHugershoff — pairing ARSTAN's deterministic fit with dplR's nonlinear-least-squares fit of the same curve. The two behave differently in each case:

  • Negative exponential. Both members minimise the same data-space error for the same model, so when the nonlinear fit converges NegExp and ModNegExp give the same curve. NegExp's advantage is robustness: being deterministic it never fails to converge, so it still returns a curve on series where the nls diverges and ModNegExp falls back to a line or the mean — handy for batch processing.
  • Hugershoff. Here the two genuinely differ: dplR's ModHugershoff minimises data-space error, while ARSTAN's Hugershoff linearises the model and minimises log-space error, so the fitted curves are not the same even when both succeed.

Other important arguments:

  • method — "ratio" (default; divide by the curve) or "difference" (subtract). Ratios are the traditional RWI; differences suit variance-stabilized workflows.
  • spline_period / f — spline stiffness (wavelength) and frequency response. spline_period defaults to a 67 %-of-length spline; a negative value is read as a percent spline (ARSTAN convention), and a value in (0, 1] as a fraction of length. f is the amplitude cutoff at that wavelength (default 0.5 = 50 %).
  • pos_slope — whether to allow a positively-sloped fitted curve.
  • plot — False by default (as in dplR's detrend for a data frame). True draws one figure per series; plot="sequential" steps through them one at a time.
  • return_info / verbose — return or print the per-series curve choices.

You can also pass a list of curves to try in order (as in dplR), and detrend a single series (pandas.Series) as well as a whole collection.

Internal gaps

dplPy fits every curve to the series with its missing years (NaN) dropped, so a -9.99-style gap value can never corrupt a fit. Spline fits a smoothing spline over the real calendar years and Mean is order-invariant. Every other fit (the parametric growth curves, the LinearAny / LinearNegative fits, and AgeDepSpline) is fitted against the true ring position year - first_year + 1, so a gap advances cambial age exactly as the calendar does and the rings after it are fit at their real age. The gap years stay NaN in the output. If you want values there, infill first with fill_internal (e.g. fill="ARSTAN", Ed Cook's opt-in regional-signal imputation) — dplPy never fills silently. See Handling internal gaps.

docs.title: rcs: regional curve standardization
docs.text:
Regional curve standardization aligns series by cambial age and divides by a single regional growth curve, preserving low-frequency (e.g. multi-centennial) signal that curve-by-curve detrending removes:

rwi = dpl.rcs(rwl, po=pith_offsets, biweight=True)             # default AgeDepSpline, ratios
rwi = dpl.rcs(rwl, po=pith_offsets, fit="Spline", spline_period=0.1)  # fixed 10%-of-length spline

The regional curve is chosen with fit= — the same curve vocabulary as detrend(): "AgeDepSpline" (the default, and ARSTAN's recommended RCS curve), "Spline", the parametric growth curves ("ModNegExp", "Hugershoff", …), or None for the unsmoothed age-aligned mean. method= selects the arithmetic ("ratio", the default, or "difference"), spline_period= sets the "Spline" stiffness (a fraction of the curve length, default 0.1; -10 is the ARSTAN percent-of-length spline), and pos_slope=False (the default) keeps the old-age end of the curve from rising. po is a pith-offset table (see po_to_wc/wc_to_po); preset="crust" builds the regional curve the CRUST way (Melvin & Briffa 2014).

Changed in 0.8.0

rcs() and sfrcs() inputs were harmonized with detrend(): the curve is now fit= (was method="caps"/"ads"), the arithmetic is method= ("ratio"/"difference", was the boolean ratios=), stiffness is spline_period= (0.8.0 called it period=, before that nyrs=; both older names still work as deprecated aliases), the default curve is fit="AgeDepSpline" (was the fixed spline), pos_slope now defaults to False, and the figure switch is plot= (make_plot= is deprecated). The pith-offset convention also changed — see the note below.

Pith-offset convention (changed in 0.8.0)

dplPy's pith_offset is a true offset: the number of rings missing between the pith and the first measured ring, so 0 means the pith is present. This is exactly ARSTAN's nshft, so an ARSTAN pith-offset file can be used directly. dplR instead stores the cambial age of the first ring (1 = pith present), so subtract 1 from a dplR pith-offset table before using it here. With no po given, dplPy assumes pith_offset = 0 (pith present) for every series.

docs.title: sfrcs: signal-free RCS
docs.text:
Ordinary RCS builds one regional curve and detrends every series by it, but when the sample's age structure varies over calendar time that curve absorbs part of the common signal and biases the low frequencies ("trend distortion"). sfrcs breaks the feedback by iterating: each pass rebuilds the regional curve from measurements that have had the current chronology divided out, while still forming the tree indices from the original measurements.

rwi = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, po=pith_offsets)
info = dpl.sfrcs(rwl, po=pith_offsets, return_info=True)  # + chronology, curve, convergence

It is a port of CRUST's single-curve signal-free RCS (Melvin & Briffa 2014) — a method with no dplR counterpart, so it is faithful to CRUST rather than validated against dplR. On CRUST's own sample data it reproduces a headless build of CRUST to about 1×10⁻³.

  • biweight_curve (default False) / biweight_crn (default False) — form the regional curve and the chronology with the arithmetic mean, matching CRUST's defaults; set either to True for a Tukey biweight robust mean.
  • ss (default 10) — the age-dependent spline stiffness offset for the curve (an 11-year minimum), as in CRUST.
  • max_iterations (default 40) / tol (default 1e-3) — the signal-free iteration budget and convergence threshold (max |Δchronology| < tol), as in CRUST. Running at max_iterations=1 performs no signal removal and reduces to one-pass CRUST RCS.

Signal-free RCS needs a wide spread of tree start dates to work well: Melvin & Briffa (2014) show distortion of the recovered signal appears once the range of starting years falls below about 200 years, and is considerable below about 100. Use it on collections whose trees germinate across a broad time range, not on a narrow single-cohort sample.

Multi-curve RCS (several regional curves with tree-to-curve allocation) is not yet implemented.

docs.title: How dplPy's RCS compares to ARSTAN
docs.text:
dplPy's rcs() matches ARSTAN single-curve RCS in its core: it aligns series by cambial age from the pith offsets, builds a robust (biweight) mean-by-age regional curve, and detrends each series by the slice of that curve at its own cambial ages, as ratios by default. A few differences are worth knowing:

  • Regional-curve shape. Like ARSTAN and CRUST, dplPy chooses the regional curve from a menu via fit=: an age-dependent spline ("AgeDepSpline", the default), a fixed smoothing spline ("Spline"), a parametric growth curve ("ModNegExp", "NegExp", "Hugershoff", "GeneralExp", "LinearAny", "LinearNegative", "Mean"), or None for the unsmoothed age-aligned mean.
