This mirrors ARSTAN's curve-fit menu — whose RCS default is likewise the age-dependent spline with a non-increasing end — and CRUST's rdt options.
  • Difference indices. With method="difference", dplPy returns residual indices centred on 0. ARSTAN instead rescales residual indices onto the ratio index's mean and standard deviation (centred on ~1). Set rescale_difference=True to reproduce that ARSTAN calind behavior per series; it is off by default, so residuals stay centred on 0.
  • Non-positive curve. If the regional curve dips to or below zero, ARSTAN halts; dplPy issues a warning and continues.
  • Pith offsets follow the +1 convention noted above.

Signal-free standardization iterates detrending and chronology-building to reduce the trend-distortion (end-effect) bias of ordinary detrending:

rwi = dpl.ssf(rwl)

It repeats until the high-frequency chronology stops changing (median absolute difference below mad_threshold). preset="crust" selects the CRUST variant.

docs.title: mrcs: multiple-curve RCS
docs.text:
A single regional curve assumes every tree shares one age->growth expectation. Because faster-growing trees tend to be younger ("grow fast, die young"), one average curve injects a slope bias when the sample's growth-rate or age mix changes over calendar time. mrcs sorts the trees by relative growth rate, splits them into a few equal-count classes, and standardizes each tree by its own class curve -- a port of CRUST's multiple-RCS option (Melvin & Briffa 2014).

rwi = dpl.mrcs(rwl, po=pith_offsets, n_curves=2)             # two growth classes
rwi = dpl.mrcs(rwl, po=pith_offsets, n_curves=3, sort="age")

Each class curve is built by rcs, so mrcs shares its curve vocabulary (fit, method, period, preset, ...) and mrcs(..., n_curves=1) is identical to rcs. Key options:

  • n_curves (default 2) -- number of regional curves. Most of the correction (and most of the low-frequency variance loss) appears already at two curves.
  • sort (default "growth") -- how trees are ranked before the split: "growth" (CRUST's growth-rate ranking), "age", "diameter", or "none".
  • reset_means (default True) -- multiple RCS removes some genuine low-frequency variance (on timescales beyond the mean tree length). With reset_means each tree's indices are rescaled back to the mean they would have had under one-curve RCS, reinstating that variance while keeping the slope correction (CRUST's "mean single"; requires method="ratio").

Use mrcs with well-replicated collections -- CRUST's rule of thumb is at least 40 trees per curve, and mrcs warns below that. The signal-free counterpart is dpl.sfmrcs, which runs the signal-free iteration (as in sfrcs) around the same growth-rate allocation; sfmrcs(..., n_curves=1) is identical to sfrcs.

docs.title: ads and powt
docs.text:
• ads fits an age-dependent spline to a single series — a spline whose stiffness increases with cambial age. It is also available inside detrend via fit="AgeDepSpline".
  • powt applies a power transformation (Cook & Peters) as an alternative to ratio detrending for variance stabilization. plot=True draws an ARSTAN-style "data transform statistics" diagnostic — per-series skew and spread-vs-level correlation, before and after the transform — and return_stats=True returns those numbers as a table, so you can check the transform actually made the series symmetric and decoupled variance from level.

docs.title: Choosing a method
docs.text: Spline and ModNegExp are the everyday choices for site chronologies. Reach for rcs when you need to retain long-timescale climate signal, sfrcs when you want RCS and the signal-free correction for trend distortion under an uneven age structure, ssf when end-effect bias matters in curve-by-curve detrending, and powt/difference detrending when heteroscedastic variance is the concern. See the Detrending & standardization reference for every parameter.

docs.title: Dating a floating series
docs.text: A floating series is undated wood — a beam from a historic building, a remnant or sub-fossil log — whose rings are measured but not yet tied to calendar years. xdate_floater estimates its calendar placement by sliding it across a dated reference collection and scoring the fit at every offset.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
You need two things:

  • a dated reference, either a whole collection (a DataFrame from readers, indexed by calendar year, from which a master chronology is built by averaging the series) or a single, already-built chronology passed as a pandas.Series or a one-column DataFrame — for example a column from read_crn; and
  • the floating series itself (a pandas.Series of ring widths; its index does not need to be calendar years).

xdate_floater builds (or takes) a master from the reference, transforms the floater the same way, and tests every alignment with at least min_overlap overlapping rings, reporting the correlation and crossdating statistics at each. The floating series may be longer than the reference.

Dating against an existing chronology. A .crn read with read_crn already is a master, so pass the column you want (e.g. crn["std"]) directly as the reference. For an already-prewhitened/residual chronology (an ARSTAN res/ars), also pass transform="none" so it is not prewhitened a second time.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import dplpy as dpl

reference = dpl.readers("reference_site.rwl", header=True)
placed = dpl.xdate_floater(reference, floating_series, series_name="beam1")

Best match for 'beam1': 1727 to 1983  (t = 17.83, r = 0.747, eff_df = 254,
p_bonf = 8.52e-44, 1/p = >1 million, IF = >1000, overlap n = 254)

If you don't pass series_name, it is taken from the series itself (a named Series, or a one-column DataFrame's column header). To date against a published chronology rather than a collection, hand it the column you want:

crn = dpl.read_crn("reference_site.crn")
placed = dpl.xdate_floater(crn["std"], floating_series, series_name="beam1")

The return value is a dictionary:

  • placed["best"] — the top-scoring placement: min_year, max_year, r, t, eff_df, p_bonf, one_over_p, isolation_factor, and n.
  • placed["floater_cor_stats"] — every tested offset, highest-t first, so you can inspect the runners-up.
  • with return_rwl=True, also placed["placed"] (the floater at its best-fit years) and placed["combined"] (floater merged with the reference).

docs.title: Reading the statistics
docs.text:
Statistic What it tells you r The sliding correlation between floater and master at that offset. t The Baillie & Pilcher (1973) t statistic, r·√(df−2)/√(1−r²). Higher is stronger; values ≥ ~3.5 are the classic acceptance threshold. eff_df Effective degrees of freedom, reduced from the raw overlap for autocorrelation (Wigley et al. 1987). p_bonf One-tailed p-value of t, Bonferroni-corrected for the many offsets tested. isolation_factor (IF) How many times larger the runner-up's p-value is than the best offset's. A large IF means the date stands out cleanly from the alternatives.

The best placement is chosen by the highest t, which accounts for the degrees of freedom at each overlap. A confident date has a high t, a tiny p_bonf, and a large isolation factor — as in the example above.

docs.title: Useful arguments
docs.text:
• min_overlap (default 50) — the minimum number of overlapping rings an alignment must have to be scored.
  • transform (default "pw") and prewhiten — how the series are detrended and prewhitened before correlation.
  • corr (default "spearman") — the correlation method.
  • series_name — a label for the floater used in the outputs and plot title; when omitted it is taken from a named series or one-column frame, else "Unknown".
  • plot=True — draw the dating figure: the sliding t and the Bonferroni-adjusted p-value against calendar year, the distribution of all t values with the best marked, and an overlay of the reference chronology against the best-placed floater over the dated overlap.

docs.title: When the best date is impossible
docs.text: dplPy also scores placements that run past the end of the reference into future calendar years — this enriches the null distribution of t values and acts as a sanity check. If the best placement lands after the present year, though, the date is impossible and the match is almost certainly spurious, so xdate_floater flags it loudly: best["date_warning"] is set to "future", a warning banner is printed (even with verbose=False), and the returned plot carries a red "best date is in the future" banner. Check the series orientation (oldest → youngest) and the reference before trusting such a result.

docs.title: No dated reference at all: xdate_undated
docs.text:
xdate_floater needs a dated reference. When there is none — a stand of sub-fossil or river-drowned trees, a pile of timbers from one structure — but the samples overlap one another in time, xdate_undated crossdates the undated series against each other and assembles them into a single, relatively dated floating chronology, in the manner of COFECHA's UFLOAT routine. It scores every pair of series at every offset with the same transform / correlation / t machinery as xdate_floater, joins series to a running mean chronology in order of strength (a series is admitted only if its best t reaches crit_t, default 4.0), sets the earliest inferred ring to anchor_year (default 1), and then re-checks every placement by leaving it out and re-dating it against the rest (verify, with an isolation score and a review flag for ambiguous placements).

floating = dpl.xdate_undated(undated_rwl, plot=True)
floating["offsets"]      # start/end of each series on the relative axis
floating["chronology"]   # the mean floating chronology
floating["unplaced"]     # series that never reached crit_t

The result is relative: the chronology (or any series in floating["placed"]) can then be dated absolutely with xdate_floater against a dated reference, or by a radiocarbon/wiggle-match anchor. See the xdate_undated reference.

docs.title: Relationship to dplR
docs.text: xdate_floater is based on dplR's xdate.floater and extends it with the t statistic and additional crossdating statistics of Wilson (2026). It differs from dplR in two documented ways: the best placement is selected by highest t (dplR uses the highest correlation r), and dplPy does not apply dplR's future-year trim — instead it tests those offsets and warns when the winning date is an impossible future one (see When the best date is impossible). See the xdate_floater reference and Coming from dplR.

docs.title: Handling internal gaps
docs.text:
An internal gap is a missing measurement (NaN) sitting between a series' first and last measured ring — a year inside the record where there is no value. They turn up for ordinary reasons: a ring obscured by rot or a scar, a damaged core segment, a value dropped in data entry, or a deliberately unmeasured stretch. This page explains what a gap means in dplPy, why it matters for some detrending methods and not others, how ARSTAN dealt with it, and — the part that matters most — how you decide what to do about it.

The guiding principle in dplPy is that an internal gap is a modelling decision, not a detail to be handled silently. dplPy will tell you when a gap could affect a result and give you the tools to deal with it, but it will never fill your data behind your back.

docs.title: A gap is not a zero
docs.text:
Two things look similar in a ring-width file but mean opposite things:

  • A measured zero is data. It records a locally absent ring — a year the tree grew so little (or not at all at that height) that no ring formed. It is dated, real, and must be kept.
  • An internal NaN is the absence of a measurement — the value is unknown.

dplPy keeps these strictly separate. dpl.readers() reads a true interior gap as NaN and a measured zero as 0.0; it never silently turns one into the other. (Older versions of dplR once substituted zero for missing — dplR no longer does this, and dplPy never did.) A measured zero is carried through detrending as a small positive index; a NaN is treated as missing everywhere.

docs.title: How each fit treats a gap
docs.text:
dplPy fits every detrending curve to the series with its NaN years dropped, so a gap can never corrupt a fit the way a sentinel value (ARSTAN's historic -9.99) could. What differs between methods is the axis the curve is fit against, and since v0.9.0 every axis is the true one:

Fit x-axis Effect of an interior gap Spline the real calendar years none beyond the missing points; the smoothing spline spans the gap in time Mean none (an average) none; order-invariant ModNegExp, NegExp, ModHugershoff, Hugershoff, GeneralExp true ring position (year - first_year + 1) none beyond the missing points; a gap advances cambial age exactly as the calendar does LinearAny, LinearNegative true ring position none beyond the missing points AgeDepSpline true ring position the gap years are infilled by carrying the last measured value forward so the age-dependent stiffness stays on the true age axis; the curve is read back only at measured rings

Before v0.9.0 the position-based fits reconstructed cambial age by counting the surviving rings 1, 2, ..., n, so every ring after a five-year gap was fit five years too young, and dpl.detrend() warned about it. That compression is gone: a ring at true cambial age 50 is fit at age 50 whether or not there is a gap before it, and no warning is needed. The same rule holds in the regional-curve functions (rcs, sfrcs, mrcs, sfmrcs), where a gap advances cambial age in the aligned matrix exactly as CRUST and dplR do, and the gap years come back as NaN in the indices rather than shifting every later year.

dplPy does not fill gaps for you

A gap stays NaN in the detrended output. If you want a value there, infill it deliberately with dpl.fill_internal() before detrending (see below) so the choice is visible in your workflow. dplPy does not change your data silently.

docs.title: How ARSTAN handled it (and why dplPy does not copy that)
docs.text:
ARSTAN filled interior gaps automatically, before any curve fitting or chronology building, and you could not turn it off. Its reader flagged negative "missing" values, and whenever any series had one it ran its fillin routine: fit each tree a flexible growth curve that glides across the gap, build a robust mean index across all the overlapping trees (the shared stand signal), and for each missing year impute a value from that common signal — rescaled to the individual tree's mean and variability and multiplied back by its growth curve. The gap came out as a modelled ring-width estimate, and standardization proceeded on a complete series. (The full mechanism, with Fortran line numbers, is in the developer note dev/arstan_gap_and_duplicate_id_2026-10-05.md.)

ARSTAN did this silently because it had to. A Fortran program of its era had no good way to hand the problem back to the user, no warnings infrastructure, and no ecosystem of helper functions — and its curve fitters summed over dense position-indexed arrays that a raw sentinel would wreck. Automatic infilling was the reasonable engineering choice at the time.

dplPy is in a different world. Python treats NaN as a first-class missing value that is dropped before fitting and skipped in aggregation, so nothing forces an infill. That lets dplPy follow a different philosophy: surface the problem, offer the options — including a faithful port of Ed Cook's own method — and let the analyst own the choice. Reproducing ARSTAN's fill is one line away when you want it; the difference is that you ask for it.

docs.title: Step 1 — find the gaps
docs.text:
dpl.readers() already flags short interior gaps on import and records every one on the dataframe:

import dplpy as dpl
rwl = dpl.readers("site.rwl")

rwl.attrs["dplpy_interior_gaps"]   # list of {series, gap years, short/long} findings

dpl.report() gives a fuller picture, listing both locally absent rings (measured zeros) and internal NaN years, per series and in total:

dpl.report(rwl)

docs.title: Step 2 — decide, then act
docs.text: There is no universally correct choice; it depends on the fit you want and how large the gaps are. The three sensible paths:

docs.title: Option A — use a spline (no infill needed)
docs.text:
If a cubic smoothing spline suits your site, just detrend. Spline spans the gap in calendar time, so no infill is required and no warning fires:

rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="Spline")
crn = dpl.chron(rwi)

docs.title: Option B — infill the gap deliberately with fill_internal
docs.text:
If you specifically want a parametric growth curve (or an age-dependent spline), infill first so the cambial-age axis is continuous, then detrend. fill_internal only touches interior NaN; leading/trailing NaN and measured zeros are left alone.

# simple, within-series fills (ports of dplR's fill.internal.NA):
filled = dpl.fill_internal(rwl, fill="Mean")     # flat at the series mean
filled = dpl.fill_internal(rwl, fill="Linear")   # straight-line interpolation
filled = dpl.fill_internal(rwl, fill="Spline")   # cubic-spline interpolation

# Ed Cook's ARSTAN method: impute each gap from the population's common signal,
# scaled to the individual series and modulated by its own growth curve:
filled = dpl.fill_internal(rwl, fill="ARSTAN")

rwi = dpl.detrend(filled, fit="ModNegExp")
crn = dpl.chron(rwi)

The simple modes interpolate within each series only and are best for short gaps where the surrounding rings carry the information. fill="ARSTAN" borrows the shared year-to-year signal from the whole collection, which is the point of Cook's method: it restores climate-like variability across the gap rather than a smooth interpolation, and is the better choice for longer gaps in a well-replicated collection. Its behaviour is tunable (growth_nyrs, long_gap, flank, stabilize), defaulting to ARSTAN's 20-year growth spline.

docs.title: Option C — accept the distortion
docs.text: For a short gap under a smooth growth curve, the age compression is often negligible. You can simply proceed with the parametric fit; the warning is a record of the decision, not an error.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("site.rwl")
dpl.report(rwl)                       # see which series have interior NaN

# You want ModNegExp curves AND a couple of series have multi-decade gaps,
# so infill with the common-signal method first, then detrend and build.
filled = dpl.fill_internal(rwl, fill="ARSTAN")
rwi    = dpl.detrend(filled, fit="ModNegExp", method="ratio")
crn    = dpl.chron(rwi)

# Compare against the no-infill spline path to see how much the choice mattered:
crn_spline = dpl.chron(dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="Spline"))

docs.title: Choosing, in short
docs.text:
Use Spline and you can ignore interior gaps entirely. Choose a parametric growth curve or an age-dependent spline and you should decide, per the gap sizes in your collection, whether to infill (and with which method) or accept a small age-axis distortion. For short gaps, fill="Spline"/"Linear" or simply proceeding is usually fine; for longer gaps in a replicated collection, fill="ARSTAN" restores realistic variability. The one thing dplPy will not do is decide for you.

See also the Detrending & standardization guide and the fill_internal reference.

docs.title: LiPD interchange
docs.text: LiPD (Linked Paleo Data) is a standard container format for paleoclimate datasets. dplPy can export a chronology (with its underlying ring widths and metadata) to a .lpd file and read one back, so dplPy results travel into the wider paleo ecosystem.

docs.title: Installing the extra
docs.text:
LiPD support is built on pylipd and is an optional extra, since most users don't need it:

pip install "dplpy[lipd]"

docs.title: Exporting with to_lipd
docs.text:
Build a chronology as usual, then write it to a .lpd file. Passing the original rwl stores the ring-width measurements alongside the chronology:

import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)
rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="Spline")
crn = dpl.chron(rwi)

dpl.to_lipd(crn, "ca533", rwl=rwl, dsname="CA533", archive_type="Wood")
# -> writes ca533.lpd

Useful arguments include dsname (the LiPD dataset name), archive_type, column (which chronology column to store), and metadata / publication / provenance for richer records. Site metadata (species, location, investigators) can be supplied via a SiteMetadata object or a metadata dict.

docs.title: Reading with from_lipd and lipd_metadata
docs.text:
from_lipd reads a .lpd file back into dplPy structures:

data = dpl.from_lipd("ca533.lpd")
data.keys()
# dict_keys(['dsname', 'rwl', 'chronology', 'chronologies', 'metadata'])

The returned dictionary contains:

  • rwl — the ring-width DataFrame (if it was stored),
  • chronology — the primary chronology (columns trsgi, sampleCount),
  • chronologies — a dict of all stored chronology types (e.g. standard),
  • metadata — the site/dataset metadata,
  • dsname — the dataset name.

To read just the metadata without loading the measurements, use lipd_metadata("ca533.lpd").

docs.title: Round trip
docs.text:
A chronology exported with to_lipd and re-read with from_lipd returns the same chronology values and ring widths, so .lpd is a lossless carrier for a dplPy analysis:

crn = dpl.chron(dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="Spline"))
dpl.to_lipd(crn, "ca533", rwl=rwl, dsname="CA533", archive_type="Wood")
back = dpl.from_lipd("ca533.lpd")
back["chronologies"]["standard"].tail()   # same chronology, round-tripped

See the utilities reference for every parameter.

docs.title: Reading & writing data
docs.text: dplPy reads the standard tree-ring file formats into a pandas DataFrame indexed by year, with one column per measurement series — the shape every other function expects. This guide covers loading ring widths, loading chronologies, combining collections, and writing data back out.

docs.title: Ring-width files with readers
docs.text:
readers loads Tucson (.rwl), CSV, and compact-format ring-width files:

import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)

ca533.rwl successfully extracted as rwl file with 34 series covering the period from 626 to 1983

Key arguments:

  • header — set True when a Tucson file carries the three ITRDB header lines, so they are read as metadata rather than data.
  • strict (default True) — mirror dplR's strict validation: dplPy warns and then raises on malformed rows, naming the offending series and year. Set strict=False to fall back to a best-effort parse that returns None on unrecoverable files instead of raising.
  • join (default True) — when a series ID appears in more than one block, join the pieces into a single column (including blocks split by a mid-file letter-case change in the ID; see Case-flipped series IDs below). dplPy reports what was merged.
  • format — normally auto-detected; override with "csv", "rwl", etc. if needed.

To load directly from a URL (for example an ITRDB file), use readers_url:

rwl = dpl.readers_url("https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/.../ca533.rwl")

NOAA template files

dplPy recognizes the *-noaa.rwl NOAA-template files and refuses them with an informative error — they are not decadal Tucson data. Use the plain .rwl file (the same name without -noaa).

docs.title: Data-quality heads-ups
docs.text:
Some files parse cleanly yet contain small oddities a human should look at. readers reads them successfully and prints a short, non-fatal heads-up (in both strict and salvage mode), with the full detail left on df.attrs for programmatic use:

  • Characters beyond the last data column. The ten decadal values occupy fixed columns 13–72; column 73 is a reserved blank separator before the optional site-ID field (columns 74–78). A non-blank character in column 73 means the last value overflowed its six-character field and was truncated — for example a 3035 written with three leading spaces leaves 5 past the column, so only 303 is read. dplPy flags these (a human must decide whether the true value was 3035 or the extra digit was a stray keystroke); content that begins at the site-ID columns (74+) is not flagged, since that is standard. Detail is on df.attrs["dplpy_beyond_column"].
  • Short interior gaps. A blank year (or two) sitting between a series' measured years — a hole in an otherwise continuous run — is often a value dropped in data entry, so dplPy flags it. Long interior gaps (many blank years in a row) are almost always intentional (a rotten or unmeasurable section, or two disjoint dated segments) and are only recorded, not announced. Every interior gap, short or long, is on df.attrs["dplpy_interior_gaps"].

These are advisories, not errors: the returned DataFrame is complete, and the missing years appear as NaN.

docs.title: Case-flipped series IDs
docs.text:
Some files write one core's ID with inconsistent letter case partway through (e.g. FDD08A for the older decades, then FDD08a). A case-sensitive read would split that into two separate series. When the case variants have disjoint years and one block is missing its stop marker — together a strong sign of a single core split by a case slip — dplPy merges them back into one series under join=True (the default) and records it on df.attrs["dplpy_case_merged"]. The merge also resolves the spurious "no stop marker" precision warning that the unterminated block would otherwise raise.

Case variants that are not merged — under join=False, or when both blocks are already properly terminated (so they may be genuinely distinct cores) — are kept separate and listed on df.attrs["dplpy_case_variant_ids"] so you can decide.

docs.title: Chronology files with read_crn
docs.text:
read_crn reads Tucson chronology (.crn) files — the standardized site chronologies produced by ARSTAN and friends:

crn = dpl.read_crn("ca533.crn")

It handles the standard single-chronology ITRDB file, the "combined" multi-block files (an ARSTAN run's stacked std/res/ars chronologies for one site), and files that concatenate many sites' chronologies. Bunched negative (BC/BCE) years parse correctly, so long chronologies read as expected. Use split_by_site=True to return separate frames per site block.

docs.title: Combining collections with combine_rwl
docs.text:
combine_rwl merges ring-width datasets onto a common year index, following dplR's combine.rwl (duplicate series IDs are kept as-is, not renamed):

both = dpl.combine_rwl(site_a, site_b)

docs.title: Writing data with writers
docs.text:
writers writes a ring-width or chronology DataFrame back to disk. Specify the output format — "rwl" (Tucson), "crn", or "csv":

path = dpl.writers(rwl, label="ca533_clean", format="rwl", prec=0.001)
print(path)        # 'ca533_clean.rwl'

writers returns the path of the file it wrote (and no longer prints a confirmation), so it composes quietly in scripts.

For .rwl output, prec sets the measurement precision (0.001 writes values ×1000 with a -9999 end marker; 0.01 writes ×100 with a 999 marker), and gaps controls how a true interior gap (a NaN inside a series' span) is encoded. See the writers reference for the full option set.

docs.title: Quick metadata
docs.text: metadata extracts the ITRDB header fields (site, species, investigators, location) from a headered Tucson file without loading the measurements, and summary/report give per-series overviews. See the Input & output reference.

docs.title: Climate–growth response
docs.text:
dpl.seascorr identifies the seasonal climate signal in a tree-ring chronology: it correlates the chronology against a primary and a secondary monthly climate variable across many candidate seasons and flags which relationships are significant. It is a faithful port of SEASCORR (Meko, Touchan & Anchukaitis 2011, Computers & Geosciences 37, 1234–1241), the first step in moving from a dated chronology toward a climate reconstruction.

The chronology is correlated (simple Pearson) with the primary variable and (partial, controlling for the primary) with the secondary variable, for every combination of a set of season-lengths and 14 ending months. Significance is assessed by exact simulation: the chronology is simulated many times in a way that preserves its spectrum, and each observed correlation is compared with the distribution of correlations from the surrogates.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
import dplpy as dpl

crn = dpl.chron(dpl.detrend(dpl.readers("site.rwl")))   # a chronology
result = dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=precip, secondary=temperature)
result.table          # one row per season: correlations, p-values, significance

crn is a year-indexed Series, or a DataFrame with column= naming the index series. primary and secondary are each one monthly climate variable. The default pairing follows the paper — precipitation primary (summed over a season), temperature secondary (averaged):

result = dpl.seascorr(
    crn, primary=precip, secondary=temperature,
    end_month=9,                      # last month of the growth year
    season_lengths=(1, 3, 6, 12),     # months; the first must be 1
    primary_agg="sum", secondary_agg="mean",
    nsim=1000,                        # exact simulations; >= 1000
    seed=42,                          # reproducible significance
)

To put temperature first (simple correlation on temperature, partial on precipitation), just swap the arguments — there is no role flag:

result = dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=temperature, secondary=precip,
                      primary_agg="mean", secondary_agg="sum")

docs.title: Climate input formats
docs.text:
Each climate variable may be supplied in whichever shape you already have; all three normalize internally to the same monthly series:

# wide: a year index/column + 12 month columns (a station CSV)
dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=wide_df, secondary=temp_df)

# tidy long: columns year, month, value
dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=tidy_df, secondary=temp_df)

# datetime-indexed monthly series (e.g. a grid-point extraction)
pre = ds["pre"].sel(lat=36.1, lon=8.5, method="nearest").to_series()
dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=pre, secondary=tmp)

Units are your responsibility (scale e.g. tenths of mm to mm before calling); primary_agg/secondary_agg then set whether a season is a sum or a mean.

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
seascorr returns a SeascorrResult. Its main payload is result.table, a tidy DataFrame with one row per season:

Column Meaning season_length, end_month, label the season (e.g. Mar–May, Oct* for a prior-year ending month) r_primary, p_primary simple correlation with the primary variable and its empirical non-exceedance probability r_partial, p_partial partial correlation with the secondary variable (controlling for the primary) and its probability r_clim Pearson r between the primary and secondary variable sig05_*, sig01_* two-sided significance flags at α = 0.05 / 0.01

Also on the result: result.highest (the strongest primary-variable season per season-length), result.acf (lag 1–5 autocorrelation of the chronology), and result.period.

docs.title: The bar chart
docs.text:
With plot=True (the default) seascorr draws the one figure the method is built around — the two-panel seasonal bar chart (simple correlations on top, partial on the bottom), significance color-coded. Bar color follows the variable: temperature is red, moisture (precipitation, PDSI, …) blue, whichever is primary. It is auto-detected from primary_name/secondary_name, and can be forced:

res = dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=temperature, secondary=precip,
                   primary_name="Temperature", secondary_name="Precipitation")
res.fig.savefig("seascorr.png", dpi=300)       # fig and axes hang off the result

# force colors, or a black-and-white version for print
dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=p, secondary=t, primary_color="blue",
             secondary_color="red")
dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=p, secondary=t, plot=True, ... )   # color=False in the plot call for B/W

Each panel's y-axis is fixed at ±0.3 and expands only to accommodate larger correlations, so a weak, non-significant partial panel still reads on a stable scale.

docs.title: Temporal stability
docs.text:
Pass an early and a late window as period to test whether the strongest season's correlation is stable between the two sub-periods (Fisher-z difference of correlations, with effective sample sizes adjusted for autocorrelation after Dawdy & Matalas 1964):

res = dpl.seascorr(crn, primary=precip, secondary=temp,
                   period=((1903, 1952), (1953, 2002)))
res.stability     # one row per season-length: r_full/early/late, Δz, p_value

A single window, period=(first, last), just sets the analysis period; omitting period uses the full overlap of chronology and climate.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Per-season significance. Each of the seasons is tested independently at its own α; seascorr does not apply a multiple-comparison correction, faithful to Meko et al. (2011). Read a lone significant season among many with that in mind.
  • Exact simulation. It is the chronology that is simulated (preserving its spectrum), so the null is "a tree-ring series with this spectrum, unrelated to climate." nsim must be at least 1000 so the tail probabilities can resolve α = 0.01. Set seed= for reproducible p-values.
  • Partial correlations behave very slightly liberally over heavily overlapping seasons; treat marginal partial-correlation significance cautiously.
  • Data requirements. The chronology must be gap-free over the analysis window and at least 31 years long (fill interior gaps with fill_internal first). Each climate variable needs complete monthly coverage over the years it contributes; because long seasons reach into the prior year, the usable window starts about two years after the first year of complete climate data.
  • Non-Gaussian chronologies still run, with a warning — the exact-simulation method assumes an approximately Gaussian series.

See the Climate response reference for the full seascorr and SeascorrResult signatures.

docs.title: Statistics & agreement
docs.text: Beyond building a chronology, dplPy provides the descriptive statistics, signal- strength measures, and agreement tests used to characterize a collection and judge whether it carries a common, datable signal.

docs.title: Descriptive statistics: stats
docs.text:
stats reports per-series summary statistics — span, mean, median, standard deviation, skew, kurtosis, the Gini coefficient, and first-order autocorrelation:

import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)
dpl.stats(rwl).head(3)

   series  first  last  year   mean  median  stdev   skew  kurtosis   gini    ar1
1  CAM011   1530  1983   454  0.440    0.40  0.222  1.029     1.102  0.273  0.696
2  CAM021   1433  1983   551  0.424    0.40  0.185  0.946     1.110  0.237  0.701
3  CAM031   1356  1983   628  0.349    0.29  0.214  0.690    -0.366  0.341  0.808

ar1 here is the autocorrelation-function coefficient at lag 1 (matching dplR's rwl.stats), not an OLS AR(1) slope.

docs.title: Mean sensitivity: sens1 and sens2
docs.text:
Mean sensitivity measures year-to-year variability. sens1 is the classic Douglass measure; sens2 is the trend-robust variant (Biondi & Qeadan 2008). Both take a single series:

s = rwl["CAM011"].dropna()
dpl.sens1(s)   # 0.3437
dpl.sens2(s)   # 0.2960

As in dplR, sensitivity is deliberately kept out of the stats table and exposed as its own functions.

docs.title: Signal strength: rwi_stats, sss
docs.text:
rwi_stats computes the population-signal statistics on detrended series — inter-series correlation (rbar), the expressed population signal (EPS), and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). It groups cores by tree using an ids table from read_ids:

rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="Spline")
ids = dpl.read_ids(rwl)
dpl.rwi_stats(rwi, ids)

   n_cores  n_trees   n  n_tot  ...  rbar_eff    eps     snr
0       34       34  34    523  ...     0.423  0.961  24.875

rwi_stats_running computes the same statistics in a moving window to see how signal strength changes through time. sss (subsample signal strength) estimates how well a reduced sample reproduces the full-collection signal — useful for deciding how far back a chronology remains reliable.

docs.title: Agreement: glk and sgc
docs.text:
glk (Gleichläufigkeit) and sgc (synchronous growth changes) measure the proportion of intervals in which two series move in the same direction — a classic non-parametric agreement test. Both return a dictionary of pairwise values and their significance:

dpl.glk(rwl, overlap=50)
dpl.sgc(rwl, overlap=50)

The p-values follow dplR's formulation (a p-value can exceed 1 when the statistic is below 0.5).

docs.title: Tree-level and interval helpers
docs.text:
• tree_mean averages cores to the tree level first (using an ids table), so multi-core trees are not over-weighted in downstream statistics.
  • common_interval finds the interval or subset of series that maximizes overlap (by years, by series, or both) — a faithful port of dplR's common.interval, handy before computing statistics that need complete data.

docs.title: Basal area increment: bai_out and bai_in
docs.text:
bai_out and bai_in convert ring widths to basal area increment, working inward from the outermost ring (bai_out) or outward from the pith (bai_in, which can take a pith-to-first-ring distance):

dpl.bai_out(rwl)
dpl.bai_in(rwl, d2pith=pith_distances)

See the Statistics & indices reference for the full parameter lists.

docs.title: Variance stabilization
docs.text:
The variance of a mean-value chronology changes through time for reasons that have nothing to do with the climate or environmental signal it is meant to carry. As sample depth grows and the mean interseries correlation shifts, the variance of the average inflates or deflates as a pure statistical artifact — early, thinly-replicated years look noisier than late, well-replicated ones. Variance stabilization removes that artifact so the chronology's variance is comparable across its whole length.

dplPy follows the ARSTAN organization: variance stabilization is a step you apply to a finished chronology, not something welded to how the chronology is built. That lets you stabilize any chronology — standard, residual, or ARSTAN — with the same engine.

docs.title: Two method families
docs.text: Two published families of methods address chronology variance, and they fix different problems. Choosing between them means diagnosing what is driving the variance change (Frank et al. 2006).

docs.title: rbar / effective sample size (theory-based)
docs.text:
The variance of a mean of correlated series scales as 1/N_eff, where the effective (independent) sample size is

\[ N_{\text{eff}} = \frac{n}{1 + (n - 1)\,\bar{r}} \]

with n the sample depth and r̄ the mean interseries correlation (Osborn et al. 1997). Stabilization scales each year's departure from the mean by sqrt(N_eff), which flattens the sample-size / correlation-driven variance trend while leaving the real common signal intact. This is the method behind ARSTAN's stabbm and Frank et al. (2006). It needs the source RWI matrix (to get r̄ and sample depth), or a precomputed r̄ and depth.

There are two sub-variants:

  • Running rbar (rbar_mode="running", the default) — r̄ is recomputed in moving windows (Frank's "RUNNINGr"). This is needed when r̄ itself trends through time, and is the widely accepted community default.
  • Constant rbar (rbar_mode="constant") — a single time-independent r̄ (ARSTAN's Briffa method; Frank's "MEANr"). Appropriate when r̄ is stable and the running estimate would only add noise.

docs.title: Spline envelope (ad hoc)
docs.text: ARSTAN's stabit fits a spline to the chronology's absolute departures, divides by that envelope, and restandardizes. It needs only the chronology — no matrix, no r̄. Because it is empirical, it flattens all time-varying variance whatever the cause, including a non-stationary component that the rbar family cannot touch (Frank et al. 2006 found exactly such residual variance and suggested the spline as the complement). The caveat (Osborn et al. 1997) is that, being ad hoc, it can also remove real low-frequency variance, so it is not theoretically clean.

docs.title: Both, in sequence
docs.text: method="both" applies the rbar correction and then a 67 % spline — the combination ARSTAN offers as menu option isb=2 and that Frank et al. (2006) recommend when both a sample-size artifact and a residual non-stationary component are present.

docs.title: stabilize_chron: stabilize any chronology
docs.text:
stabilize_chron takes a chronology you already built with chron or chron_ars and returns the stabilized version. The method is explicit and required, because the families do different things:

import dplpy as dpl

rwi = dpl.detrend(dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True), fit="Spline")
crn = dpl.chron(rwi)                       # a standard chronology

# rbar / N_eff scaling with the running rbar of the source matrix
vsc = dpl.stabilize_chron(crn, "rbar", rwi=rwi)
vsc.tail(3)

           vsc  samp_depth
Year
1981  1.238...          21
1982  1.331...          21
1983  1.297...          21

The stabilized chronology comes back in a vsc column (plus samp_depth when known). Key arguments:

  • method — "rbar", "spline", or "both" (required).
  • rwi — the source RWI matrix, used to derive r̄, the running r̄, and sample depth for the rbar family. For a residual or ARSTAN chronology, pass the residual (prewhitened) matrix (see below).
  • rbar / running_rbar / samp_depth — precomputed inputs, as an alternative to passing rwi.
  • rbar_mode — "running" (default) or "constant".
  • spline_period, f — spline stiffness and frequency response for the "spline" / "both" families (None = the 67 % spline, ARSTAN's default).
  • column — which column to stabilize when passing a DataFrame (default "std").
  • return_info — return a dict instead of the bare chronology: the stabilized chronology under "chron" plus diagnostics (the r̄ used, N_eff, and sample depth).

Passing only the chronology (no matrix) is enough for the spline family:

vsc = dpl.stabilize_chron(crn, "spline")   # needs only the chronology

docs.title: The stabilize= flag on chron and chron_ars
docs.text:
For convenience, both chron and chron_ars accept a stabilize= argument so you can build and stabilize in one call. Each base chronology gets a stabilized sibling column beside it (std_vsc, res_vsc, ars_vsc), mirroring ARSTAN, where the menu stabilization option applies to every chronology it produces:

# standard + residual chronologies, each with a stabilized version
crn = dpl.chron(rwi, prewhiten=True, stabilize="both")
list(crn.columns)
# ['std', 'std_vsc', 'res', 'res_vsc', 'samp_depth']

# all three ARSTAN chronologies, each stabilized
ars = dpl.chron_ars(rwi, stabilize="both")
list(ars.columns)
# ['std', 'std_vsc', 'res', 'res_vsc', 'ars', 'ars_vsc', 'samp_depth']

Pass extra options through stabilize_kwargs:

crn = dpl.chron(rwi, stabilize="rbar",
                stabilize_kwargs={"rbar_mode": "constant"})

The defaults (running rbar, 67 % spline) match Frank et al. (2006) and ARSTAN. stabilize=None (the default) leaves the output exactly as it was without the flag.

docs.title: Per-chronology rbar
docs.text: Following ARSTAN's convention, each chronology is stabilized with the rbar of the matrix it came from: the standard chronology uses the rbar of the standard (detrended) RWI matrix, and the residual and ARSTAN chronologies use the rbar of the residual (prewhitened) matrix. The stabilize= flags handle this automatically; when calling stabilize_chron directly, pass the appropriate matrix as rwi=.

docs.title: The ARSTAN chronology is stabilized before re-reddening
docs.text: ARSTAN stabilizes the residual chronology and then re-reddens it, so chron_ars(stabilize=...) does the same: with ars_method="arstan" (the default), the residual chronology is stabilized before the pooled AR persistence is reintroduced (ars_vsc = postAR(res_vsc)). This keeps ars_vsc consistent with the unstabilized ars and faithful to ARSTAN. (With ars_method="dplr", the ARSTAN chronology is already built by re-reddening each series and averaging, so ars_vsc is stabilized post-hoc on the reddened chronology.) See Building chronologies for the ars_method distinction.

docs.title: chron_stabilized: the dplR-parity path
docs.text:
chron_stabilized is dplPy's port of dplR's chron.stabilized. Unlike stabilize_chron, it takes the RWI matrix and builds its own standard mean-value chronology internally, applying the running-rbar / N_eff correction as it goes:

crn = dpl.chron_stabilized(rwi, window_length=50, min_seg_ratio=1/3)

It is the right choice when you want exact dplR parity for the standard chronology. For a residual or ARSTAN chronology, for the spline or "both" families, or to stabilize a chronology you already built, use stabilize_chron or the stabilize= flag.

docs.title: A note on rescaling
docs.text:
Both families restandardize the stabilized chronology to the input chronology's full-period mean and standard deviation. This differs from ARSTAN's stabbm, which rescales to a user-chosen reference period. The full-period convention keeps the stabilized chronology on the same overall scale as the input while removing the time-varying variance; see Fidelity & departures for the rationale.

chron_stabilized follows dplR instead: it scales the departures by sqrt(N_eff * rbar) and adds the grand mean back, which places the chronology on the variance an infinitely replicated chronology would have (Osborn, Briffa & Jones 1997). The two conventions flatten the same variance trend and differ only by a uniform level and scale (on ca533 the running-rbar outputs are related by a slope of 1.11 and an offset of -0.12, with a residual below 0.002 that comes from centring the matrix before rather than after the biweight mean). Spline mode is identical between the two. The difference is invisible to correlation-based uses and visible wherever absolute index values are read off, such as pointer-year thresholds or a plot that overlays a dplR-stabilized chronology.

docs.title: Choosing a method
docs.text: Frank et al. (2006) recommend diagnosing the source of the variance change before choosing — inspect the variance of individual, age-aligned series. Use the running-rbar method for variance driven by changing sample size or interseries correlation; use the spline for a residual, non-stationary component the rbar family cannot explain; and use "both" when both are present. See the Chronology reference for full parameter lists and References for the source literature.

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text: Averaging detrended series into a site chronology, with optional autoregressive modelling and variance stabilization. See the Building chronologies guide.

docs.title: chron
docs.text:
Build a mean-value chronology from ring-width indices.

Averages the series (detrended RWI) year by year into a standard chronology, optionally prewhitening each series with an AR model first to also produce a residual chronology. Mirrors dplR's chron().

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rwi_data pandas dataframe

detrended ring-width indices (e.g. from dpl.detrend()).

required biweight boolean

average with Tukey's biweight robust mean if True, else the arithmetic mean.

True prewhiten boolean

prewhiten each series with an AR model to also build a residual chronology.

False plot boolean

plot the chronology.

True ar_max int

maximum AR order considered when prewhiten is True. To reproduce dplR's chron() exactly, pass ar_max=floor(10*log10(n)) and first_aic_min=False. (max_lag= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

10 aic boolean

when prewhiten is True, select the AR order by AIC up to ar_max; if False, fit a fixed AR of order ar_max.

True ar_method (yw, burg, ols)

AR estimator for prewhitening (case-insensitive). "yw" (Yule-Walker) matches R's ar() default; "burg" is ARSTAN's estimator; "ols" matches R's ar(method="ols").

"yw" first_aic_min boolean

AR order-selection rule when aic is True. True takes the first local AIC minimum (ARSTAN's rule, dplPy's package default); False takes the global AIC minimum, which is what R's ar() and dplR's chron() do.

True backcast boolean

when prewhiten is True, fill each series' first p residuals with ARSTAN-style backcast initials so no years are lost. False (default) leaves them NaN, as R's ar() residuals and dplR's chron() do.

False stabilize (None, rbar, spline, both)

if set, also variance-stabilize each chronology and return the stabilized versions in extra *_vsc columns (see Notes). Method families are as in stabilize_chron().

None stabilize_kwargs dict

extra keyword arguments forwarded to stabilize_chron() when stabilize is set. The chronology, column, source RWI matrix, and sample depth are supplied automatically and may not be overridden here.

None ci boolean

also compute a bootstrap confidence interval for the standard chronology, adding lower_ci and upper_ci columns. Each year's available series are resampled R times and the normal-approximation interval of the bootstrap means is taken. Years with fewer than two series get NaN limits (with a warning). The interval is only for the standard chronology.

False conf float

confidence level, used when ci is True.

0.95 R int

number of bootstrap replicates per year, used when ci is True (dplR's chron.ci default).

100 seed int or None

seed for the ci bootstrap, for reproducible intervals.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description data pandas dataframe

a mean-value chronology indexed by year (the full year index of rwi_data), with columns std (standard chronology), res (residual chronology, only when prewhiten is True), and samp_depth. A year with no series present has NaN chronology values and samp_depth 0, as in dplR. With ci=True, lower_ci and upper_ci columns for the standard chronology. When stabilize is set, a stabilized *_vsc column is added next to each base chronology.

Notes

Prewhitening. Each series is whitened with autoreg._prewhiten(), the package-wide prewhitening (Yule-Walker, ar_max=10, first local AIC minimum). This differs from R's ar()/dplR, which take the global AIC minimum up to floor(10*log10(n)); pass first_aic_min=False and ar_max accordingly to reproduce dplR.

Variance stabilization (stabilize). The standard chronology is stabilized with the rbar of the standard RWI matrix and the residual chronology with the rbar of the residual matrix; both restandardize to the full period (see stabilize_chron()). For the re-reddened ARSTAN chronology, use chron_ars() with stabilize=.

Examples:

>>> import dplpy as dpl
>>> rwi_data = dpl.detrend(dpl.readers("../tests/data/csv/file.csv"))
>>> dpl.chron(rwi_data)
>>> dpl.chron(rwi_data, prewhiten=True)
References

.. [1] https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/chronology/#chron

docs.title: chron_stabilized
docs.text:
Build a variance-stabilized mean-value chronology.

Scales a mean-value chronology by the square root of the effective independent sample size Neff = n(t) / (1 + (n(t)-1) rbar(t)), where n(t) is the sample depth and rbar(t) the mean pairwise interseries correlation, computed over windows of length window_length. Port of dplR's chron.stabilized().

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rwi_data DataFrame

detrended ring-width indices.

required window_length int

window length over which rbar values are calculated. (win_length= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

50 min_seg_ratio float

minimum ratio of non-NA values to window length for a series to count in an Neff calculation (⅓ matches dplR's chron.stabilized()).

1/3 biweight boolean

average with Tukey's biweight robust mean if True, else the arithmetic mean.

True running_rbar boolean

also return the running rbar values in the output (only for method='running_rbar').

False method str

the variance-stabilization method (case-insensitive):

  • 'running_rbar' : running-window-rbar effective-signal adjustment (Frank et al. 2006 "RUNNINGr"); the default. Uses window_length and min_seg_ratio.
  • 'briffa' (alias 'mean_rbar') : the same adjustment with a single time-constant rbar over all pairwise overlaps longer than 20 years (Osborn et al. 1997; Frank et al. 2006 "MEANr"). Corrects for changing sample size only.
  • 'spline' : ARSTAN's ad-hoc spline stabilization, removing any time trend in the absolute departures with a smoothing spline. Can remove real low-frequency variance -- use with care. Stiffness set by spline_period.
'running_rbar' spline_period (int, float or None)

stiffness for method='spline'. An int > 1 is a fixed spline wavelength in years; a float in (0, 1) is a fraction of the chronology length; None uses the 67% spline (floor(0.67*n) years, as stabilize_chron and dplR's detrend default; earlier releases used 0.5n). Ignored by the rbar methods. (spline_nyrs= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

None

Returns:

Name Type Description stabilized_chron pandas dataframe

a variance-stabilized mean-value chronology indexed by year, with columns vsc, running_rbar (only when running_rbar=True), and samp_depth. Years with no series present have samp_depth 0 and NaN vsc.

Notes

This function scales the departures and adds the grand mean back, as dplR does; stabilize_chron() instead restandardizes to the input chronology's full-period mean and SD, so the two differ slightly in level and scale.

Examples:

>>> import dplpy as dpl
>>> data = dpl.readers("../tests/data/csv/file.csv")
>>> dpl.chron_stabilized(data, window_length=60, min_seg_ratio=0.4)
References

.. [1] https://rdrr.io/cran/dplR/man/chron.stabilized.html .. [2] https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/chronology/#chron_stabilized

docs.title: stabilize_chron
docs.text:
Variance-stabilize an already-built chronology.

Scales the departures of a chronology you already built with chron() or chron_ars() (standard, residual, or ARSTAN) to remove time-varying variance. Unlike chron_stabilized(), which takes the RWI matrix and builds its own standard chronology, this takes the finished chronology.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default chron Series or DataFrame

the chronology to stabilize. A Series is used directly; a DataFrame (e.g. chron()/chron_ars() output) uses column and, if present, its samp_depth column.

required method (rbar, spline, both)

required, explicit (case-insensitive):

  • "rbar" -- Osborn (1997) / Frank (2006) N_eff scaling; corrects variance driven by changing sample size (and, with running rbar, changing interseries correlation). Needs sample depth and rbar.
  • "spline" -- ARSTAN's ad-hoc absolute-departure spline; flattens all time-varying variance whatever the cause, and can remove real low-frequency variance. Needs only the chronology.
  • "both" -- "rbar" then a 67% "spline", in sequence.
"rbar" column str

which column to stabilize when chron is a DataFrame.

"std" rwi DataFrame

the source ring-width-index matrix (for the "rbar" family); rbar, running rbar, and sample depth are derived from it. For a residual or ARSTAN chronology pass the residual (prewhitened) matrix.

None rbar float

precomputed scalar rbar (for rbar_mode="constant" without rwi).

None running_rbar array - like

precomputed per-year running rbar (for rbar_mode="running" without rwi).

None samp_depth array - like

per-year sample depth. Taken from the DataFrame's samp_depth column or from rwi when not given.

None rbar_mode (running, constant)

running rbar (Frank RUNNINGr) or a single time-constant rbar (Osborn/Briffa MEANr).

"running" window_length (int, float)

running-rbar window length (default 50; must be shorter than the chronology) and minimum overlap ratio (as in chron_stabilized). (win_length= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

50 min_seg_ratio (int, float)

running-rbar window length (default 50; must be shorter than the chronology) and minimum overlap ratio (as in chron_stabilized). (win_length= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

50 spline_period (int, float or None)

spline stiffness for the "spline"/"both" families. None = the 67% spline (floor(0.67*n) years); an int > 1 is a fixed wavelength in years; a float in (0, 1) is a fraction of length; a negative value is a percent spline.

None f float

spline frequency response (50% amplitude cutoff).

0.5 clip_negative bool

clamp the stabilized chronology at >= 0.

True return_info bool

also return the diagnostics (rbar used, N_eff, sample depth).

False

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

indexed by year, with the stabilized chronology in column vsc and, when known, samp_depth. If return_info is True, returns a dict instead, with the DataFrame under "vsc" plus "method", "rbar", "n_eff" and "samp_depth" (the latter three for the rbar family).

Notes

Both families restandardize to the input chronology's full-period mean and SD, so the stabilized chronology stays on the scale you already had. dplR's chron.stabilized (ported as chron_stabilized()) instead scales the departures by sqrt(n_eff * rbar) and adds the grand mean back, which puts the chronology on the variance of an infinitely replicated chronology (Osborn, Briffa & Jones 1997). The two flatten the same variance trend and differ only by a uniform level and scale (on ca533: slope 1.11, offset -0.12, residual below 0.002), which matters for anything read off absolute index values but not for correlation-based uses. For the ARSTAN chronology, stabilization must precede re-reddening, so use chron_ars(stabilize=...) rather than calling this on an already re-reddened series.

References

Osborn, Briffa & Jones (1997) Dendrochronologia 15, 89-99. Frank, Esper & Cook (2006) TRACE 4, 56-66.

docs.title: chron_ars
docs.text:
Build ARSTAN standard, residual, and re-reddened chronologies.

Produces the three ARSTAN chronologies of Cook (1985) from a set of detrended ring-width indices:

  • std: the standard chronology, the (robust) mean of the RWI series with no autoregressive modeling.
  • res: the residual chronology, each series prewhitened by an AR(p) model of the pooled order, averaged, then prewhitened once more to order p (near-white).
  • ars: the ARSTAN chronology, the pooled red-noise persistence reintroduced by re-reddening; ars_method sets how (see Notes).

The pooled AR order p is selected by AIC from an autocovariance accumulated across all series. Analog of dplR's chron.ars.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rwi_data pandas dataframe

detrended ring-width indices (e.g. from dpl.detrend), years as the index and series as columns. Columns with no measured values are dropped with a warning.

required biweight boolean

aggregate series with Tukey's biweight robust mean if True, else the arithmetic mean.

True ar_max int

maximum AR lag considered when selecting the pooled AR order. (max_lag= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

10 first_aic_min boolean

select the order at the first local AIC minimum (ARSTAN's and dplR's rule) if True, else the global AIC minimum. With True, a pooled AIC that never turns back up within ar_max raises ValueError.

True verbose boolean

print the pooled ACF, AR coefficients, AIC, and selected order.

True prewhiten_method str

estimator for the per-series (and residual-chronology) AR(p) whitening, case-insensitive: "ar.yw" (Yule-Walker; numerically exact match to dplR), "burg" (Burg maximum entropy, ARSTAN's estimator) or "arima.CSS-ML" (matches dplR within tolerance).

"ar.yw" ars_method str

how the re-reddened ARSTAN chronology is built (see Notes): "arstan" re-reddens the residual chronology, reproducing Ed Cook's ARSTAN and the current dplR development version; "dplr" re-reddens each prewhitened series then averages, reproducing released dplR <= 1.8.0.

"arstan" backcast boolean

backcast the initial values of each AR whitening and re-reddening step (ARSTAN's bckcst) so no leading years are lost. False sets the first p residuals of every series to NaN, as dplR's chron.ars does, and re-reddens from zero initials. Applies to the "ar.yw" and "burg" paths; "arima.CSS-ML" already returns full-length residuals.

True stabilize (None, rbar, spline, both)

if set, also variance-stabilize each chronology and return the stabilized versions in extra *_vsc columns (see Notes). Method families are as in stabilize_chron().

None stabilize_kwargs dict

extra keyword arguments forwarded to stabilize_chron() when stabilize is set. The chronology, column, source matrix, and sample depth are supplied automatically and may not be overridden here.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description out pandas dataframe indexed by year with columns 'std', 'res', 'ars', and

'samp_depth'. When stabilize is set, a stabilized std_vsc, res_vsc, and ars_vsc column is added next to each base chronology.

Notes

ARSTAN chronology (ars_method). ARSTAN whitens every series to the pooled order p, averages them, whitens that mean once more (the residual chronology, albino1), and then puts the pooled persistence back into the residual chronology (commie1): ars = redden(res, phi_pooled). That is ars_method="arstan" (default), and also what the dplR development version computes. Released dplR <= 1.8.0 instead re-reddened each prewhitened series and averaged those; ars_method="dplr" reproduces it. Re-reddening and averaging do not commute when sample depth changes through time, so the two differ; the std and res columns, the pooled AR order, and the prewhitening are identical either way.

Backcasting (backcast). An AR(p) filter has no data for its first p lagged terms. With backcast=True (default) those pre-sample values are estimated by running the model in reverse from the start of each series (ARSTAN's bckcst), so the residual and ARSTAN chronologies are full length (no leading NaN); the first p years of each series are model-based, so treat them as slightly less certain. With backcast=False the first p residuals of every series are NaN, as in dplR's chron.ars. Because series start in different years, that changes the chronology res (and ars) in every year where some series is within its first p years -- not only the first p years of the chronology. dplR's postAR took its re-reddening initials from the end of the record; dplPy follows ARSTAN here too, so ars differs from dplR in roughly the first 10 years of each series' contribution.

Variance stabilization (stabilize). std_vsc uses the rbar of the standard RWI matrix; res_vsc the rbar of the residual matrix; ars_vsc is the stabilized residual chronology re-reddened ("arstan") or the reddened chronology stabilized with the residual rbar ("dplr"). Each column restandardizes to its own full period (see stabilize_chron()).

Examples:

>>> import dplpy as dpl
>>> rwi = dpl.detrend(dpl.readers("../tests/data/csv/file.csv"), plot=False)
>>> dpl.chron_ars(rwi)
References

.. [1] https://rdrr.io/cran/dplR/man/chron.ars.html .. [2] Cook, E.R. (1985) A time series analysis approach to tree-ring standardization. PhD dissertation, University of Arizona. .. [3] https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/chronology/#chron_ars

docs.title: autoreg
docs.text:
Fit the best-fit AR model to a series and return its parameters.

Selects the AR order up to max_lag by AIC and returns the fitted model parameters.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Series

an individual series representing tree rings/widths.

required ar_max int

maximum AR order considered when selecting the model. (max_lag= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

10 aic bool

select the AR order by AIC up to ar_max; if False, fit a fixed AR of order ar_max.

True method (yw, burg, ols)

AR estimator. "yw" (Yule-Walker) is dplPy's package default and matches R's ar() default and dplR; "burg" is the estimator ARSTAN and COFECHA use; "ols" matches R's ar(method="ols").

"yw" first_aic_min bool

when aic is True, True takes the first local AIC minimum (ARSTAN's rule, dplPy's package default), False the global minimum. NOTE this default differs from R's ar() / dplR, which take the global minimum.

True

Returns:

Name Type Description params array

parameters of the best-fit AR model, as [intercept, phi_1, ..., phi_p].

Examples:

>>> import dplpy as dpl
>>> data = dpl.readers("../tests/data/csv/file.csv")
>>> dpl.autoreg(data["series name"])
References

.. [1] https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/chronology/#autoreg

docs.title: ar_func
docs.text:
Prewhiten series with a best-fit AR model.

Fits each series to the best-fit autoregressive model and returns the residuals plus the series mean (the prewhitened series).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data DataFrame or Series

ring widths from dpl.readers(), or a single series taken from one.

required ar_max int

maximum AR order considered when selecting the model. (max_lag= is accepted as a deprecated alias.)

10 aic bool

select the AR order by AIC up to ar_max; if False, fit a fixed AR of order ar_max.

True method (yw, burg, ols)

AR estimator. "yw" (Yule-Walker) is dplPy's package default and matches R's ar() default and dplR; "burg" is the maximum-entropy estimator ARSTAN and COFECHA use; "ols" matches R's ar(method="ols").

"yw" first_aic_min bool

when aic is True, True takes the first local AIC minimum (ARSTAN's rule, dplPy's package default), False the global minimum. NOTE this default differs from R's ar() / dplR, which take the global minimum.

True

Returns:

Name Type Description res pandas dataframe or series

the prewhitened data (residuals plus mean), matching the input type. The first p values of each series (the AR warm-up) are dropped, so a Series comes back p shorter and a DataFrame has NaN there. Columns with no measured values are dropped with a warning.

Examples:

>>> import dplpy as dpl
>>> data = dpl.readers("../tests/data/csv/file.csv")
>>> dpl.ar_func(data["series name"])
References

.. [1] https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/chronology/#ar_func

docs.title: Climate response
docs.text: Correlation of a tree-ring chronology with monthly and seasonal climate (SEASCORR; Meko, Touchan & Anchukaitis 2011), and reconstruction of climate from a tree-ring network by orthogonal spatial / principal-components regression (OSR; Cook, Briffa & Jones 1994). See the Climate–growth response guide for worked examples, and Reconstruction validation for how pcreg validates a reconstruction and what each statistic in result.stats means.

docs.title: seascorr
docs.text:
Seasonal correlation of a tree-ring chronology with monthly climate.

A faithful port of SEASCORR (Meko, Touchan & Anchukaitis 2011). The chronology is correlated (simple Pearson) with a primary climate variable and (partial, controlling for the primary) with a secondary variable, across season-lengths x 14 ending months. Significance is assessed by exact spectral simulation of the chronology.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default crn Series or DataFrame

One monthly climate variable each, in any of three shapes: wide (year index/column + 12 month columns), tidy (year, month, value), or a monthly datetime/period-indexed series.

(1, 3, 6, 12) primary_agg (sum, mean)

How each variable is aggregated over a season (sum for totals such as precipitation, mean for temperature).

"sum" secondary_agg (sum, mean)

How each variable is aggregated over a season (sum for totals such as precipitation, mean for temperature).

"sum" nsim int

1000 period None, (first, last), or ((e0, e1), (l0, l1))

Analysis window. A single pair sets the window; a pair of pairs sets an early and a late window and triggers the stability test.

None seed int or None

Seed for the surrogate random generator (reproducible significance).

docs.title: pcreg
docs.text:
Orthogonal spatial regression / PC-regression climate reconstruction.

A faithful port of Ed Cook's OSR FORTRAN (Cook, Briffa & Jones 1994). The predictors are screened against the target over the calibration window, reduced to principal components, and the target is regressed on the PCs that pass a t-test; the fit is back-transformed to per-predictor weights, a reconstruction is produced over the full predictor period, and (if a validation window is given) it is validated against the withheld data.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default predictors DataFrame or Series

Year-indexed tree-ring predictors (e.g. the output of :func:read_crn). Sample-depth companion columns are dropped automatically.

required target Series or 1-column DataFrame

Year-indexed climate target to reconstruct. Pre-seasonalize it yourself (e.g. a March-May PDSI mean) before calling.

required calibration (first, last)

Calibration window, inclusive.

required validation (first, last) or None

Validation window, inclusive. When None, only the calibration fit and the reconstruction are returned (no validation statistics).

None screen_alpha float

Screening significance level. Use 1.0 with screen_tails=2 to force every predictor into the PCA ("normal response function").

0.1 screen_tails (1, 2)

One- or two-tailed screening test.

1 screen_sign ('+', '-', None)

Required correlation sign for a one-tailed test.

'+' min_coverage int or None

Minimum overlapping years to admit a predictor. Defaults to the full calibration length (every predictor must cover the whole window), which is what the fixture uses.

None pc_criterion (pvp, kaiser, first_m, cum_pct, all)

PC truncation rule (Cook's eigenvalue-cutoff options 3, 1, 0, 2, 4).

'pvp' n_pc int

Number of PCs for pc_criterion='first_m'.

12 ev_cutoff float

Rescaled-eigenvalue cutoff for pc_criterion='kaiser'.

1.0 cum_pct float

Cumulative-variance percent for pc_criterion='cum_pct'.

90.0 order_method tstat

PC entry/stop rule. Phase 1 implements the t-statistic rule.

'tstat' t_cutoff float

|t| threshold for order_method='tstat'.

1.0 prewhiten bool

Prewhiten predictors and target with a best-fit AR model before screening (reuses :func:dplpy.autoreg.ar_func). The AR order is chosen by AIC up to ar_max.

False ar_max int

Maximum AR order when prewhiten=True.

10 ar_method (burg, yw, ols)

AR estimator. 'burg' (maximum entropy) matches Cook's memcof.

'burg' lag None, 11-char mask string, or sequence of int

Lead/lag the predictors before screening (Cook's lagit). Each predictor is expanded into one column per offset: offset d uses the predictor at year Y + d to predict year Y (d < 0 = a lag on earlier ring years, d > 0 = a lead). Give the offsets directly (e.g. (0, 1) or (-1, 0, 1)) or as an 11-char mask over positions -5..+5 (e.g. "00000110000" = offsets 0 and +1). The same mask is applied to every predictor.

None cv None or int

Cross-validate by refitting the whole pipeline on held-out folds of the calibration period. cv=1 is leave-one-out; cv=k leaves out contiguous k-year blocks. Results land in stats under the cv_ keys (cv_r, cv_RE, cv_CE; cv_RE and cv_CE coincide over the calibration window). None skips cross-validation.

None first_differences bool

Also report validation statistics on the 1st-differenced series (the FORTRAN's second validation pass), under _diff keys in stats.

True plot bool

Draw the reconstruction/validation figure.

False

Returns:

Type Description PcregResult Notes

A single target, PC-regression core with optional AR prewhitening, lead/lag predictor masks, 1st-difference validation, and leave-k-out cross-validation. Deferred to a later phase (and documented in dev/pcreg_DECISIONS.md): canonical regression, robust / biweight correlations, and the Southern-Hemisphere auto-shift.

docs.title: PcregResult
docs.text:
Result of :func:pcreg.

Attributes:

Name Type Description reconstruction Series

Year-indexed reconstruction of the target over the full predictor period, in the target's own units (variance rescaled to the calibration mean and SD).

calibration, validation tuple(int, int) or None

The calibration and validation windows (first, last).

predictors_screened list

Column labels retained by the screening step, in column order.

screen_info DataFrame

Per-predictor r, t and p from screening.

n_pc int

Number of principal components retained.

pcs_selected list of int

1-based PC numbers entered in the regression, in entry order.

cal_r2 float

Calibration R-squared.

stats dict

Validation statistics on the undifferenced data, the same set on the 1st-differenced data under _diff keys, and -- when cv was requested -- the cross-validated skill under cv_ keys. The panel mirrors Cook's verify: RE, CE; Pearson r (r_p); spearman and kendall rank correlations (_p); the robust biweight midcorrelation (robust_p); the sign_pos/sign_neg sign test (sign_p); the product-means test pm_diff (pm_t, pm_p); and the equality-of-means test eqmeans_diff (eqmeans_t, eqmeans_p). Significance comes from SciPy's exact distributions; the correlation p-values are one-sided (positive skill expected) and the sign test is an exact binomial. robust is the modern biweight midcorrelation (equivalent to astropy's), which replaces Cook's older sum/difference robcor.

cv_reconstruction Series or None

The pooled held-out cross-validation prediction per calibration year (target units), or None when cv was not requested.

dropped_coverage list

Predictor columns excluded before screening for insufficient calibration coverage (with lead/lag, because the lagged window runs past their data). Reported as a warning at fit time; kept here for inspection.

weights Series

Back-transformed weight per screened predictor.

eigenvalues ndarray

Original eigenvalues of the screened-predictor correlation matrix (descending).

settings dict

The resolved analysis settings.

docs.title: Crossdating
docs.text: Statistical crossdating against a master chronology, COFECHA-style batch reporting, floating-series dating, and relative dating of undated collections. See the Crossdating & COFECHA and Dating a floating series guides.

docs.title: xdate
docs.text:
Crossdate a set of ring-width series against a leave-one-out master.

Each series is normalized, optionally AR-prewhitened, and correlated against a biweight master built from all the other series, over segments of window_length years overlapping by half. Mirrors dplR's corr.rwl.seg.

Flagged segments are labelled A or B (mutually exclusive):

  • B -- the segment correlates better at a non-dated lag (best lag != 0): a possible dating shift. (dplR flags on significance only; dplPy adds this COFECHA-style lag flag, also used by preset="COFECHA".)
  • A -- lag 0 is the best match but the correlation is not significant (one-tailed p >= p_val): weak but correctly placed.

Lag sign: the dated segment stays fixed and the master slides past it, so a negative lag means a missing ring in the series (as in COFECHA). The same convention holds in series_corr and check.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data DataFrame

detrended RWI (e.g. from dpl.detrend). With preset="COFECHA" pass the RAW ring-width frame instead; the preset detrends internally, so do not pre-detrend.

required prewhiten bool

AR-prewhiten each series (autoreg._prewhiten: Yule-Walker, order by the first local AIC minimum up to ar_max; the first order years of a series become NaN as in dplR).

True corr (spearman, pearson, kendall)

correlation method (case-insensitive).

"spearman" window_length int

segment length in years (slide_period= is a deprecated alias).

50 bin_floor int

the first segment is floored to a multiple of this.

100 p_val float

significance level for the A flag.

0.05 biweight bool

build the master with a Tukey biweight robust mean (else arithmetic).

True lag int

maximum ± lag examined for the B flag.

10 show_flags bool

print the summary box, the flag summary and lag tables.

True plot bool

draw the segment-correlation plot.

False preset str or None

"COFECHA" (case-insensitive) emulates the COFECHA program instead of dplR. Pass the RAW frame (the preset detrends and variance-stabilizes it itself): it uses Pearson correlation, a z-scored arithmetic leave-one-out master, 50-year segments on a 25-year grid anchored to each series' span, a 99% one-tailed-t critical value, Burg AR prewhitening, and a lag search that slides the master past the dated segment. Adds the segments key; corr, biweight, bin_floor and p_val are ignored.

None seg_lag int or None

segment step in years (overlap). None uses window_length // 2. Preset only.

None ar_max int or None

AR-order ceiling for prewhitening (ARSTAN/COFECHA's 10). None uses dplR's floor(10*log10(n)).

10 first_aic_min bool

pick the AR order at the first local AIC minimum (the ARSTAN/COFECHA rule, dplPy's package default) rather than the global minimum. ar_max=None, first_aic_min=False reproduces dplR's corr.rwl.seg prewhitening exactly. Ignored by the COFECHA preset (always first-minimum, Burg).

True absent DataFrame or None

COFECHA preset only -- marks locally absent rings to omit from a series' correlations. A boolean (years x series) frame, or a raw ring-width frame whose zeros mark them (e.g. absent=raw_rwl == 0). None disables the omission.

None spline_period int

COFECHA preset only -- spline wavelength (years) for the internal detrend and variance stabilization (stabilize_period= is a deprecated alias).

32

Returns:

Type Description dict

with keys:

  • seg_corr -- DataFrame (series x bins) of segment correlations
  • p_val -- DataFrame (series x bins) of one-tailed p-values
  • overall -- DataFrame (series x ['rho', 'p_val']), the correlation with the leave-one-out master
  • avg_seg_corr -- Series (bins), mean correlation across series
  • flags -- dict {series: {'A': [...], 'B': [...]}}, each entry a dict {segment, best_lag, best_corr, lags} where lags is the list of correlations at lags -lag..+lag (floats, NaN where untestable)
  • bins -- list of "start-end" bin labels
  • rwi -- DataFrame of the normalized/prewhitened series used (attrs["kind"] == "rwi")
  • n_problems -- int, the number of flagged segments (A + B)
  • summary -- dict, the header-box statistics (n_series, first_year, last_year, span, total_rings, dated_rings_checked, intercorrelation, mean_sensitivity, n_problems, mean_series_length)

With preset="COFECHA" also:

  • segments -- dict {series: [{lo, hi, r0, best_lag, best_corr, n, crit, flag, lags}]}
  • preset -- "COFECHA"

Examples:

>>> rwi = dpl.detrend(ca533, fit="spline", plot=False)
>>> res = dpl.xdate(rwi)
>>> res = dpl.xdate(rwl, preset="COFECHA")   # pass the RAW frame
>>> res["n_problems"]
References

.. [1] https://opendendro.github.io/dplPy/reference/crossdating/#xdate

docs.title: xdate_report
docs.text:
Generate a COFECHA-style crossdating QA report for one or more .rwl files.

For each file: read (salvage mode), detrend, cross-date with dpl.xdate, collate per-series statistics, and print the report and/or save it as <name>.txt in out_dir (see output). Built for batch QA of ITRDB submissions. Pass preset="COFECHA" to emulate the COFECHA program instead (Burg prewhitening, spline variance stabilization, an arithmetic z-scored master, Pearson correlation, COFECHA segment anchoring and critical value, and "omit absent rings" fed from the raw frame); pass a RAW frame in that case.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default files str, pandas.DataFrame, or list

A .rwl path, an already-loaded ring-width DataFrame (e.g. from dpl.readers()), or a list mixing either. A DataFrame is reported directly (the read step is skipped). For the COFECHA preset, pass a RAW frame (zeros marking absent rings).

required out_dir str

Directory for the .txt reports (created if needed).

"." fit str

detrending curve passed to dpl.detrend (ignored when preset="COFECHA", which always uses a spline).

"Spline" corr

passed through to dpl.xdate (corr, bin_floor and p_val are ignored when preset="COFECHA"; window_length still applies). slide_period= is a deprecated alias of window_length.

'spearman' window_length
